items.title: HIPAA Privacy, Security, and Breach Notification Rules — business associate obligations
items.citation: 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164; Privacy Rule 164.502(e)/164.504(e); Security Rule 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314; Breach Notification Rule 164.402, 164.404, 164.410
items.applies_to_vendor: A vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information (PHI) on behalf of a HIPAA covered entity (or another business associate) is itself a 'business associate' and must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with each covered-entity/BA client (45 CFR 164.504(e), 164.314(a)). As a business associate, LOVELEEDAY is directly liable under the Security Rule's administrative, physical, and technical safeguards (164.308/164.310/164.312) and must notify the covered entity of any breach of unsecured PHI without unreasonable delay, and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery (164.410(b)).
key_obligations: Sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with every covered-entity or upstream-business-associate client before receiving PHI (45 CFR 164.504(e))
Conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis of potential risks/vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI (45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A))
Implement risk management measures to reduce identified risks to a reasonable level (164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B))

Apply the Security Rule's administrative, physical, and technical safeguards (access controls, audit controls, encryption where appropriate, workforce sanctions, information system activity review) (164.308, 164.310, 164.312)

Notify the covered entity of a breach of unsecured PHI without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery, including identification of affected individuals to the extent possible (164.410(a)-(c))
Only use/disclose PHI as permitted by the BAA and report unauthorized use/disclosure to the covered entity (164.504(e)(2))
items.notice_deadline: Business associate to covered entity: "without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach" (45 CFR 164.410(b))
items.regulator_notice: The covered entity (not the business associate directly, unless the BAA delegates it) must notify HHS OCR; for breaches affecting 500+ individuals, notice to HHS is required contemporaneously with individual notice, and to prominent media outlets serving the affected jurisdiction (164.408).
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Protected health information' (PHI) = individually identifiable health information held/transmitted by a covered entity or business associate, in any form (45 CFR 160.103). 'Unsecured PHI' (the breach-notification trigger) means PHI not rendered unusable/unreadable/indecipherable via HHS-specified encryption/destruction methods.
items.penalties: HHS OCR civil monetary penalties under the HITECH Act tiered structure (per-violation amounts that adjust annually for inflation, ranging from roughly hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars per violation depending on culpability tier, with an annual cap per identical violation type); willful neglect can also trigger DOJ criminal referral.
items.effective_or_amended: HIPAA Security Rule most recently proposed for major update in 2025 (NPRM); Breach Notification Rule from 2009 (HITECH), largely unchanged since 2013 Omnibus Rule.
items.uncertainty: HHS.gov's own BAA/Security Rule guidance pages returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches this session; the regulatory text itself was fetched and verified directly from ecfr.gov instead, which is the authoritative source. Exact current civil-penalty dollar tiers were not independently re-verified this session (HHS 403'd); do not quote a specific number without a fresh HHS/Federal Register check.

how_to_comply.step: Sign a Business Associate Agreement with each covered-entity (or upstream business associate) client before touching PHI
Conduct and document a HIPAA Security Rule risk analysis covering all systems that create/receive/maintain/transmit ePHI
Implement the Security Rule's required/addressable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards and document a remediation plan for gaps
Build and rehearse a breach-detection and 60-day covered-entity notification workflow
Flow BAA-equivalent terms down to any subcontractor (e.g., cloud host) that will also touch PHI (164.308(b)(1))

items.attestation: Signed BAA; a documented risk analysis; buyers increasingly also ask for a SOC 2 Type II report or HITRUST certification as evidence, though neither is a HIPAA legal requirement
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of a HIPAA covered entity or another business associate client
items.not_triggered_when: The client is not a HIPAA covered entity/business associate, or LOVELEEDAY never receives health information (e.g., pure billing/scheduling metadata with no health content)
items.effort: high — a signed BAA per client, a documented risk analysis, a real administrative/physical/technical-safeguards program, and a rehearsed 60-day breach-notification process; this is the heaviest-effort item in this set.

items.title: 42 CFR Part 2 — Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records; Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA)
items.citation: 42 U.S.C. 290dd-2; 42 CFR Part 2, definitions at 42 CFR 2.11
items.applies_to_vendor: Part 2 governs records of federally assisted substance use disorder (SUD) treatment programs — a stricter confidentiality regime than HIPAA. A vendor providing services (e.g., data processing) to a Part 2 program is a 'qualified service organization' (QSO) only if it has a written Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA) with the Part 2 program under which it (1) acknowledges it is fully bound by Part 2's regulations in receiving/storing/processing patient records, and (2) will, if necessary, resist in judicial proceedings any effort to obtain unauthorized access to patient-identifying information, disclosing only that a court order exists (42 CFR 2.11).
key_obligations: Sign a written Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA) with each Part 2 program client (42 CFR 2.11)
Acknowledge in the QSOA that LOVELEEDAY is fully bound by 42 CFR Part 2 when receiving, storing, processing, or otherwise dealing with patient records
Agree to resist, in judicial proceedings, efforts to obtain access to patient-identifying SUD information beyond what the regulations/QSOA permit
Do not redisclose SUD patient-identifying information except as permitted by Part 2 (general rule: no redisclosure without specific written patient consent or a qualifying exception)
items.regulator_notice: Complaints of noncompliance may be filed with HHS in the same manner as HIPAA complaints (42 CFR 2.4(b), referencing 45 CFR 160.306) following 2024 rule changes that aligned Part 2 enforcement with HIPAA.
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Protects 'records' of any individual who has applied for or received SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral for treatment from a federally assisted Part 2 program — broader confidentiality than general HIPAA PHI in that even the existence of treatment is protected.
items.penalties: Criminal fines for disclosure violations under 42 U.S.C. 290dd-2; since the 2024 rule alignment, HHS OCR also applies HIPAA's civil-penalty enforcement structure to Part 2 breach-notification and enforcement provisions.
items.effective_or_amended: 2024 final rule (89 FR 12472, Feb. 16, 2024) substantially aligned Part 2 with HIPAA
items.uncertainty: Did not locate/verify the specific section number establishing the QSOA as a disclosure exception (distinct from the §2.11 QSO definition itself) within this session's page fetch; the definitional text at §2.11 is confirmed, but the operative permitting-disclosure section should be re-confirmed before drafting an actual QSOA.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm whether the health-industry client is a federally assisted SUD ('Part 2') program as opposed to a general health provider
Sign a Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA) with the Part 2 program before receiving any SUD patient records
Layer Part 2's stricter redisclosure limits on top of the existing HIPAA BAA safeguards program (see us-hipaa-business-associate-obligations)

items.attestation: Signed Qualified Service Organization Agreement (QSOA)
items.triggered_when: The health-sector client is a federally assisted substance use disorder program and LOVELEEDAY receives, stores, or processes SUD patient-identifying records
items.not_triggered_when: The client is a general health provider with no federally assisted SUD program, or LOVELEEDAY never touches SUD-specific patient records
items.effort: medium — mainly a signed QSOA; the underlying technical safeguards largely overlap with the HIPAA Security Rule program already required for any health client.

items.title: 2 CFR Part 200 (Uniform Guidance) — obligations that flow down to contractors of federally funded grantees
items.applies_to_vendor: Uniform Guidance governs how a nonprofit or local-government 'recipient'/'subrecipient' of federal grant funds spends that money, including on vendors. Under 200.331, LOVELEEDAY is almost always a 'contractor' (procuring goods/services within LOVELEEDAY's normal business operations, offered to many customers, not subject to the federal program's own compliance requirements) rather than a 'subrecipient' (which carries the recipient's own full compliance burden, including single-audit exposure). As a contractor, LOVELEEDAY is not directly regulated by Uniform Guidance, but the client (as recipient/subrecipient) must (a) maintain procurement oversight to ensure LOVELEEDAY performs per contract terms (200.318(b)), and (b) give the federal awarding agency, Inspectors General, the Comptroller General, or a pass-through entity 'timely and reasonable' access to LOVELEEDAY's records pertinent to the federal award, and to LOVELEEDAY's personnel for interviews about them (200.337(a)) — a right that lasts as long as the records are retained, not just for the standard retention period.
key_obligations: Accept the client's contractual right of oversight to ensure LOVELEEDAY performs per the terms, conditions, and specifications of the contract (200.318(b))

Provide the federal awarding agency, Inspectors General, Comptroller General, pass-through entity, or their authorized representatives timely and reasonable access to LOVELEEDAY records pertinent to the federal award, and to relevant personnel for interview, for as long as those records are retained (200.337(a))

Support the client's records-retention schedule (generally three years from submission of the final expenditure report, longer in specified circumstances) for anything pertinent to the award (200.334)

Accept any federally required flow-down contract clauses the client must include (e.g., equal-opportunity, debarment, whistleblower-protection clauses from 2 CFR Part 200 Appendix II) even though LOVELEEDAY itself is a contractor, not a subrecipient
items.penalties: No direct federal penalty runs against a contractor under Uniform Guidance; enforcement runs against the recipient/subrecipient (the client), which can face disallowed costs, funding conditions, suspension, or debarment for procurement or oversight failures — consequences that flow back into the vendor relationship contractually, not through direct federal action against LOVELEEDAY.
items.effective_or_amended: 89 FR 30136, April 22, 2024 (most recent Uniform Guidance revision)
items.uncertainty: The exact list of Appendix II flow-down clauses potentially applicable to a given LOVELEEDAY contract was not independently pulled this session; the general oversight/records-access/retention framework (200.318, 200.331, 200.334, 200.337) is directly sourced and confirmed.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm with the nonprofit/local-government client whether the specific engagement is paid from a federal award, and whether LOVELEEDAY is being treated as a contractor (normal case) or a subrecipient
Accept a records-access clause giving the federal agency/pass-through entity/Inspectors General/Comptroller General timely access to records pertinent to the award, for as long as they're retained
Match LOVELEEDAY's own records-retention practice to the client's federal retention schedule for anything pertinent to the award (generally 3 years from final expenditure report)
Review and accept any Appendix II flow-down clauses the client's grant terms require in the vendor contract

items.attestation: No federal attestation form for a 'contractor' (as distinct from a 'subrecipient'); the procurement contract/purchase order itself, plus any required Appendix II flow-down clauses, is the instrument
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is under contract to a nonprofit or local-government client that is a recipient or subrecipient of federal grant funds, and LOVELEEDAY's services are paid for in whole or part from that federal award
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is paid from the client's unrestricted/non-federal funds, or the relationship is structured (correctly, per 200.331(b)) as a standard commercial contractor arrangement rather than a subrecipient relationship
items.effort: low for a normal contractor relationship (records-access clause + retention alignment); would become high only if LOVELEEDAY were misclassified as a 'subrecipient,' which pulls in full Uniform Guidance subpart F single-audit exposure — worth confirming contractor status explicitly in each grant-funded contract.

items.title: ADA Title II Rule — Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps of State and Local Government
items.citation: 28 CFR Part 35, Subpart H (§§35.200–35.207), as amended by 89 FR 31320 (Apr. 24, 2024) and the 2026 Interim Final Rule extending compliance dates
items.applies_to_vendor: The legal duty runs to the state/local government entity, not directly to LOVELEEDAY, but a vendor building a public-facing website or app for a covered government client must deliver content conforming to WCAG 2.1 Level AA so the government client can meet its own compliance date.
key_obligations: Web content and mobile apps that state/local governments provide or make available must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA
Government entities with total population of 50,000 or more must comply by April 26, 2027 (per 2026 Interim Final Rule, extended from April 24, 2026)
Government entities with total population under 50,000, or any special district government, must comply by April 26, 2028 (extended from April 26, 2027)
Limited exceptions exist (e.g., archived web content, preexisting conventional electronic documents, certain third-party content, individualized password-protected documents)
items.penalties: DOJ/private-party ADA Title II enforcement (injunctive relief, compensatory damages in some circumstances) against the government entity; a vendor's noncompliant deliverable exposes the government client, and by extension the vendor, to contractual liability.
items.effective_or_amended: Final rule April 24, 2024; compliance dates extended by 2026 Interim Final Rule
items.uncertainty: Did not independently confirm the exact April 2026 Interim Final Rule Federal Register citation number; relied on ada.gov's summary of the extended dates.

how_to_comply.step: Build all client-facing web content and mobile apps delivered to local-government clients to conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA success criteria
Track each government client's population-based compliance deadline (April 26, 2027 for population ≥50,000; April 26, 2028 for <50,000/special districts) and schedule remediation/testing before it
Run automated + manual accessibility testing (screen reader, keyboard-only navigation, color contrast) before each government-facing release and document conformance for the client's compliance file

items.attestation: WCAG 2.1 AA conformance report / VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) the government client will request from LOVELEEDAY
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY builds or maintains a public-facing website, portal, or mobile app for a state or local government client
items.not_triggered_when: The deliverable is purely internal/back-office tooling never exposed to the public, or content falls under a named Title II exception (e.g., true archival content)
items.effort: medium-high — WCAG 2.1 AA conformance requires design and engineering discipline (semantic HTML, contrast, keyboard nav, ARIA) but is achievable without third-party certification

items.title: Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act — ICT Accessibility for Federally Funded Technology
items.citation: 29 U.S.C. § 794d; 36 CFR Part 1194 (Revised 508 Standards, incorporating WCAG 2.0/2.1 Level AA by reference)
items.applies_to_vendor: A vendor providing information and communication technology (ICT) that a federal agency (or a state/local program built with federal funds and subject to a Section 508 flow-down clause) develops, procures, maintains, or uses must ensure that ICT conforms to the Revised 508 Standards.
key_obligations: Conform ICT (software, websites, electronic documents) to the Revised 508 Standards, which generally require WCAG 2.1 Level AA conformance
Complete an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR)/VPAT when requested during federal or federally-funded procurement
Support the federal agency's annual Section 508 conformance reporting obligations by supplying accurate accessibility documentation
items.penalties: Federal agency may reject or terminate procurement of noncompliant ICT; complaints can be filed with the agency or the U.S. Access Board
items.effective_or_amended: Revised 508 Standards; phased compliance deadlines extended by one year in 2026 per section508.gov
items.uncertainty: Section 508 binds federal agencies directly; whether it flows down to LOVELEEDAY depends on the specific federal-funding agreement or grant terms the local-government client operates under — did not confirm a specific flow-down clause.

how_to_comply.step: Determine whether the local-government client's project is federally funded with a Section 508 flow-down requirement in the grant/contract
Build ICT deliverables to conform with the Revised 508 Standards (WCAG 2.1 AA) under 36 CFR Part 1194
Prepare an Accessibility Conformance Report (VPAT) documenting conformance for the procuring agency

items.attestation: Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR/VPAT)
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's software is procured, developed, or used by a federal agency, or by a state/local government program under a contract/grant that flows down Section 508 requirements
items.not_triggered_when: The client and funding source are purely state/local with no federal funding or flow-down clause (ADA Title II governs instead)
items.effort: medium — largely the same WCAG 2.1 AA engineering work as the ADA Title II item, plus producing a VPAT document

items.title: DFARS 252.204-7012 — Safeguarding Covered Defense Information and Cyber Incident Reporting
items.applies_to_vendor: A contractor or subcontractor whose contract includes this clause and who has Covered Defense Information (CDI, a form of CUI) on its internal information system must implement NIST SP 800-171 security requirements on that system, and report cyber incidents affecting CDI or the contractor's ability to perform to DoD within 72 hours of discovery.
key_obligations: Provide 'adequate security' on all covered contractor information systems that process, store, or transmit covered defense information
Implement NIST SP 800-171 security requirements (or document deviations in a System Security Plan and Plan of Action & Milestones)
Rapidly report cyber incidents to DoD within 72 hours of discovery via the DoD DIBNet portal, and preserve/provide forensic images on request
Flow the clause down to subcontractors whose effort will involve covered defense information
Maintain the required CMMC assessment level as a condition of award for contracts that incorporate the CMMC clause
items.notice_deadline: 72 hours of discovery of a cyber incident
items.regulator_notice: Report via DIBNet (DoD-designated portal) to DoD, not a state AG
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Covers 'Covered Defense Information,' a category of CUI — not personal information specifically, though CDI can include technical data, operationally critical support info, and CUI categories that overlap with PII
items.penalties: Contract termination for default, False Claims Act exposure for misrepresenting compliance, ineligibility for award
items.effective_or_amended: Clause version referenced: MAY 2024

how_to_comply.step: Confirm whether any DoD prime/subcontract LOVELEEDAY holds or will hold includes DFARS 252.204-7012 and whether LOVELEEDAY's system will process Covered Defense Information
Implement the NIST SP 800-171 security requirements on the information system that touches CDI and document a System Security Plan (SSP) and Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) for any gaps
Register in the DoD DIBNet portal and stand up an incident-reporting process able to report within 72 hours of discovery
Flow the clause down to any subcontractor that will handle covered defense information on LOVELEEDAY's behalf

items.attestation: Self-assessment score submitted to the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS), SSP/POA&M, and — where the contract requires it — a CMMC certificate/self-assessment
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY holds a DoD contract or subcontract (including as a manufacturing/distribution software vendor to a defense supplier) that flows down DFARS 252.204-7012 because covered defense information will be processed, stored, or transmitted
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's manufacturing/distribution clients are entirely commercial with no DoD prime or subcontract, or the information involved is not CDI/CUI
items.effort: high — implementing all applicable NIST SP 800-171 controls (110 requirements under Rev 2) across a production environment is a significant security-engineering undertaking

items.title: NIST SP 800-171 — Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems
items.citation: NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2 (Feb 2020, currently the DoD/CMMC-referenced baseline) and Rev. 3 (May 2024, final)
items.applies_to_vendor: A nonfederal organization (including a software vendor to a manufacturer/distributor) that processes, stores, or transmits Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) on behalf of a federal agency, or as a DoD contractor/subcontractor under DFARS 252.204-7012, must implement the security requirements in SP 800-171.
key_obligations: Implement the 110 security requirements (Rev 2) or the updated/renumbered requirement set (Rev 3) across 14 control families: access control, awareness & training, audit & accountability, configuration management, identification & authentication, incident response, maintenance, media protection, personnel security, physical protection, risk assessment, security assessment, system & communications protection, system & information integrity
DoD contracts currently reference Rev 2 via the CMMC rule; Rev 3 is the current NIST publication and agencies are expected to transition over time
Document implementation status and any unimplemented requirements in a System Security Plan (SSP) and Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M)
Submit a Basic Assessment score to DoD's Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS) for applicable contracts
items.personal_info_definition_notes: CUI can include export-controlled technical data, proprietary manufacturing/business information, and in some categories personal information tied to a federal program — determined by the CUI Registry.
items.penalties: Loss of contract eligibility; False Claims Act liability for false compliance attestations; part of CMMC assessment failure
items.effective_or_amended: Rev. 3 finalized May 2024 (Rev 2, Feb 2020, remains the DoD/CMMC reference version)
items.uncertainty: Did not independently confirm which revision (2 vs 3) any specific current DoD contract clause references at this moment; per public reporting, CMMC 32 CFR Part 170 references Rev 2 as of this writing.

how_to_comply.step: Scope which LOVELEEDAY systems store/process/transmit CUI for a manufacturing/distribution client's federal or DoD-flow-down work
Implement the applicable SP 800-171 security requirement families on those systems (access control, encryption, audit logging, incident response, etc.)
Complete a self-assessment against SP 800-171A, score it, and submit the score to SPRS if required by contract

items.attestation: SPRS self-assessment score; SSP and POA&M; CMMC Level 2 certificate/self-assessment where required
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's software stores, processes, or transmits Controlled Unclassified Information for a manufacturing/distribution client performing on a federal or DoD contract
items.not_triggered_when: The manufacturing/distribution client's use of LOVELEEDAY's product is purely commercial, with no CUI or federal contract flow-down involved
items.effort: high — same underlying control set as DFARS 252.204-7012; a multi-month security program build-out for a small vendor

items.title: Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) Program
items.applies_to_vendor: A DoD contractor or subcontractor that will process, store, or transmit Federal Contract Information (FCI) or CUI must achieve and maintain the CMMC Status (Level 1, 2, or 3) specified in the contract before award and throughout performance; the level required flows down to subcontractors based on what CUI/FCI they will handle.
key_obligations: Level 1 (Foundational): annual self-assessment against 15 basic safeguarding requirements (for FCI only)
Level 2 (Advanced): the 110 requirements from NIST SP 800-171 R2, via either a third-party (C3PAO) assessment or, for a defined subset of contracts, self-assessment
Level 3 (Expert): the Level 2 requirements plus 24 additional requirements from NIST SP 800-172, assessed by the Defense Industrial Base Cybersecurity Assessment Center (DIBCAC)

A subcontractor that will process/store/transmit CUI must hold at minimum CMMC Level 2 (Self); if the prime contract requires Level 2 (C3PAO) or Level 3 (DIBCAC), the subcontractor's minimum status is still Level 2 (C3PAO) per 32 CFR 170.23
Annual affirmation of continued compliance by a senior company official
items.penalties: Ineligibility for contract award; False Claims Act exposure for false affirmations of CMMC status
items.effective_or_amended: 32 CFR Part 170 — current eCFR version
items.uncertainty: CMMC contract-clause rollout (DFARS 252.204-7021) phase-in schedule for when specific contracts start requiring it was not independently re-verified this session.

how_to_comply.step: Determine the CMMC level required by the specific DoD prime contract or subcontract LOVELEEDAY supports, based on whether FCI or CUI is involved
For Level 1, complete and annually renew a self-assessment against the 15 FCI safeguarding requirements
For Level 2, implement all NIST SP 800-171 R2 requirements and engage a C3PAO for a third-party assessment (or self-assess if the specific contract allows)
Have a senior company official submit the annual affirmation of continued compliance in the DoD supplier portal

items.attestation: CMMC Status certificate (Level 1/2 self-assessment or Level 2 C3PAO / Level 3 DIBCAC certificate) recorded in the DoD supplier system
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY is a subcontractor (directly or via a manufacturing/distribution client) on a DoD contract that requires CMMC status because FCI or CUI will be processed, stored, or transmitted
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's manufacturing/distribution clients have no DoD contracts, or the LOVELEEDAY product never touches FCI/CUI
items.effort: high for Level 2/3 (third-party or DIBCAC assessment, full NIST 800-171/800-172 control implementation); low-medium for Level 1 (self-assessment against 15 basic controls)

items.title: ITAR — Export Control of Technical Data Related to Defense Articles
items.citation: 22 CFR Parts 120–130 (International Traffic in Arms Regulations); definition of 'technical data' at 22 CFR 120.33
items.applies_to_vendor: If LOVELEEDAY's software stores, transmits, or provides access to ITAR-controlled technical data (data required for the design, development, production, or maintenance of a defense article on the U.S. Munitions List) on behalf of a manufacturing client, LOVELEEDAY becomes subject to ITAR's controls on 'export,' including release to a foreign person wherever located, and may need to register with the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC).
key_obligations: Identify whether any client data qualifies as 'technical data' (design, development, production, operation, repair, or maintenance information) for a USML-listed defense article
Prevent 'deemed export' — do not give any foreign-person employee, contractor, or cloud-region access to ITAR technical data without a license or applicable exemption

Register with DDTC if LOVELEEDAY itself manufactures, exports, or brokers defense articles/services (registration is generally not required for a data processor that merely hosts data under an exemption, but access controls are still required)
Store/segregate ITAR technical data in access-controlled, U.S.-person-only environments
items.penalties: Civil penalties up to statutory maximums per violation and criminal penalties (fines and imprisonment) under the Arms Export Control Act; debarment from future defense contracts
items.uncertainty: Whether LOVELEEDAY registration with DDTC is required (vs. an exemption applying) is a fact-specific legal determination outside the scope of this general item; flag for counsel review before onboarding any client whose data may include USML technical data.

how_to_comply.step: Screen new manufacturing clients and their data for USML-controlled technical data before onboarding; do not accept ITAR technical data into a system not built for it
If ITAR data will be handled, restrict system access to verified U.S. persons only and geofence hosting to U.S. data centers/regions
Consult export-control counsel on whether LOVELEEDAY must register with DDTC or qualifies for an exemption, before signing a contract that involves ITAR technical data

items.attestation: No standard third-party certificate; a buyer may ask for an ITAR compliance/export-control policy, U.S.-person-only access attestation, or DDTC registration number if applicable
items.triggered_when: A manufacturing client's data stored or processed by LOVELEEDAY includes technical data for a defense article on the U.S. Munitions List
items.not_triggered_when: The manufacturing client makes only commercial (non-defense) products, or LOVELEEDAY never receives design/production/technical data tied to a USML article — the default assumption for most LOVELEEDAY manufacturing clients
items.effort: high if triggered (access segregation, U.S.-persons-only staffing, possible DDTC registration); most LOVELEEDAY manufacturing clients should aim to stay in the 'not triggered' state by contract scope

items.title: EAR — Export Control of Dual-Use Technology and Technical Data
items.citation: 15 CFR Parts 730–774 (Export Administration Regulations); scope at 15 CFR Part 734
items.applies_to_vendor: If LOVELEEDAY's software stores, transmits, or provides foreign-person access to export-controlled 'technology' (as defined and classified under an Export Control Classification Number on the Commerce Control List) on behalf of a manufacturing/distribution client, LOVELEEDAY must treat any release of that technology to a foreign person — including within the U.S. cloud environment — as a 'deemed export' subject to EAR licensing requirements.
key_obligations: Determine the Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) of any controlled technology/technical data a client asks LOVELEEDAY to store or process
Treat visual/oral/written release of controlled technology or source code to a foreign person as an export requiring a license or applicable exception (15 CFR 734.15)
Screen for restricted parties/countries before granting system access to controlled technology
Maintain export-control compliance procedures if regularly hosting EAR-controlled technology
items.penalties: Civil and criminal penalties under the Export Control Reform Act, administered by BIS; denial of export privileges
items.uncertainty: EAR classification (ECCN determination) is fact-specific per product/technology and was not performed here; this item states the general framework only.

how_to_comply.step: Ask manufacturing/distribution clients whether the data/technology LOVELEEDAY will host is subject to an ECCN under the Commerce Control List

If controlled technology is involved, restrict access (including cloud-region and support-staff access) to authorized/screened persons and countries, treating any foreign-person access as a deemed export requiring a license or exception
Screen users/clients against BIS restricted- and denied-party lists before granting access

items.attestation: No standard third-party certificate; a buyer may ask for an export-control compliance policy or ECCN determination for the data involved
items.triggered_when: A manufacturing/distribution client's data hosted by LOVELEEDAY includes EAR-controlled technology/technical data (dual-use or otherwise controlled under the Commerce Control List)
items.not_triggered_when: The client's technology/data is EAR99 (not separately controlled) or purely commercial business data with no export-controlled technical content — the default for most LOVELEEDAY manufacturing clients
items.effort: medium-high if triggered (ECCN determination, access screening); low if LOVELEEDAY's contract scope stays limited to non-controlled business/operations data

items.title: TCPA — Restrictions on Telemarketing Calls and Text Messages
items.applies_to_vendor: If LOVELEEDAY builds or operates SMS/voice marketing/notification features for a hospitality or retail client, LOVELEEDAY (as the platform enabling the calls/texts) shares exposure with the client for TCPA-compliant consent capture, since the FCC treats text messages as 'calls' under the TCPA and 64.1200 requires prior express written consent for autodialed/prerecorded marketing calls and texts.
key_obligations: Obtain prior express written consent — a signed (including electronic) agreement clearly authorizing autodialed/prerecorded marketing calls or texts — before sending marketing messages via an automatic telephone dialing system or prerecorded voice
For non-marketing informational calls/texts, obtain at least prior express consent
Honor opt-out requests and maintain internal do-not-call lists; transmit accurate caller ID/telemarketer identification information
Design consent-capture and opt-out flows so the client can demonstrate compliant consent records if challenged
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Phone numbers and consent records are the core data elements at issue.
items.penalties: Private right of action, statutory damages per violation (higher for willful/knowing violations), plus FCC enforcement
items.uncertainty: Did not confirm the current exact dollar-penalty figures, which are indexed periodically; consult FCC's current guidance before quoting a number to a client.

how_to_comply.step: Build the SMS/voice feature so that a client cannot enable marketing sends to a contact without a stored, timestamped record of prior express written consent
Implement automatic honoring of STOP/opt-out keywords and suppress further sends to opted-out numbers
Pass accurate caller ID / sender identification through any calling feature

items.attestation: No formal certificate; clients/carriers (via 10DLC registration) will ask for documented consent-capture and opt-out workflows
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's product sends or enables a hospitality/retail client to send marketing or informational SMS/voice messages using an automatic telephone dialing system or prerecorded voice
items.not_triggered_when: All messaging is one-to-one, manually dialed, non-marketing, and outside TCPA's autodialer/prerecorded-voice triggers (a narrow carve-out; treat most bulk messaging features as in-scope)
items.effort: medium — mainly a product/consent-UX design requirement, not a certification, but must be built correctly from the start

items.title: CAN-SPAM Act — Commercial Email Requirements
items.applies_to_vendor: If LOVELEEDAY builds or operates email-marketing features for hospitality/retail clients, the platform must support the CAN-SPAM requirements the client is legally obligated to meet for every commercial email.
key_obligations: Do not use false or misleading header/from/subject-line information
Clearly identify the message as an advertisement (where applicable) and include the sender's valid physical postal address
Provide a clear and conspicuous opt-out mechanism in every commercial email, and honor opt-out requests within the statutory processing window without charge
Not sell or transfer the recipient's email address after an opt-out, except to a service provider helping comply with CAN-SPAM
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Email addresses and opt-out status are the key data elements.
items.penalties: FTC civil penalties per violation (email), private right of action for some ISPs, and criminal penalties for aggravated violations
items.uncertainty: Did not independently verify the current per-email civil penalty amount, which the FTC periodically adjusts for inflation.

how_to_comply.step: Build email-sending features so every commercial email template requires a valid physical postal address and a working one-click unsubscribe link
Process opt-out requests automatically and suppress the address from future sends within the statute's processing window, without requiring payment or additional information beyond the email address
Do not allow header/subject-line spoofing in the platform's send configuration

items.attestation: No formal certificate; email service providers (e.g., for deliverability) will review compliant sending practices
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's product sends or enables a hospitality/retail client to send commercial (marketing) email
items.not_triggered_when: All email is purely transactional (e.g., receipts, reservation confirmations) with no promotional content, which CAN-SPAM treats differently (lighter requirements, but still must avoid false header information)
items.effort: low — mostly a product-template requirement (address, unsubscribe link) rather than a certification

items.title: ADA Title III — Website Accessibility for Public Accommodations (no final DOJ regulation)
items.citation: 42 U.S.C. §§ 12181–12189 (Title III); DOJ's Title III implementing regulations at 28 CFR Part 36 — no web-specific technical standard has been adopted
items.applies_to_vendor: Honest legal position: DOJ has never issued a final Title III regulation setting a specific technical accessibility standard (such as WCAG) for websites of private businesses ('public accommodations'); DOJ withdrew its prior rulemakings on the subject. DOJ's longstanding informal guidance is that Title III's general nondiscrimination and effective-communication requirements apply to websites, and courts (not a regulation) have overwhelmingly required WCAG-level conformance in practice, driving a large volume of private ADA website litigation against hospitality and retail businesses. LOVELEEDAY should build to WCAG 2.1 AA as the de facto litigation-risk-reducing standard, while being accurate with clients that no DOJ rule mandates it.
key_obligations: No DOJ Title III regulation currently specifies a technical web-accessibility standard — this is DOJ's own stated position

DOJ's 'Guidance on Web Accessibility and the ADA' states the general nondiscrimination/effective-communication provisions of Title III apply to websites of public accommodations, without prescribing a specific technical standard

In practice, courts overwhelmingly reference WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA as the evidentiary benchmark in Title III website litigation, so building to that standard is the practical way to reduce litigation exposure even though it is not a codified legal requirement
items.penalties: Private lawsuits (often high-volume, plaintiff's-bar-driven) seeking injunctive relief and attorney's fees; no direct DOJ civil penalty scheme has been triggered by lack of a specific web rule
items.effective_or_amended: DOJ's Title III web rulemakings have been withdrawn; most recent DOJ guidance dated 2022
items.uncertainty: This is an accurate statement of the regulatory gap as of this session, not legal advice; case law differs across federal circuits on whether/how Title III applies to websites with no physical nexus.

how_to_comply.step: Build hospitality/retail client-facing websites and apps to conform with WCAG 2.1 (or current 2.2) Level AA as a practical risk-reduction standard, while telling clients honestly that this is not a codified DOJ requirement for Title III
Ensure effective communication alternatives exist (e.g., accessible contact methods) consistent with Title III's general nondiscrimination requirement

items.attestation: No formal certificate; a VPAT/WCAG conformance statement is the practical document clients request
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY builds a public-facing website or app for a hospitality or retail client that is a 'place of public accommodation' under Title III
items.not_triggered_when: Purely internal/back-office tooling with no public-facing surface
items.effort: medium — same WCAG 2.1 AA engineering discipline as the government items above, done here as risk mitigation rather than a codified mandate

items.title: Fair Housing Act — Nondiscriminatory Advertising, as it Touches Property-Management Software
items.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD implementing regulations, 24 CFR Part 100
items.applies_to_vendor: If LOVELEEDAY builds listing, advertising, tenant-matching, or ad-targeting features for a property-management/real-estate client, those features must not make, print, publish, or cause a notice, statement, or advertisement that indicates a preference, limitation, or discrimination on a protected basis (race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, national origin) to an 'ordinary reader/listener,' regardless of intent — including HUD's specific guidance on digital ad-targeting platforms.
key_obligations: Do not build listing/ad copy or image tools that convey a preference/limitation based on a protected class

Do not build or expose ad-targeting/audience-selection features (e.g., for a client's digital ad campaigns) that allow exclusion of protected classes or proxies for them (e.g., zip codes correlated with race) from seeing housing ads — HUD's 2024 guidance on digital-platform advertising specifically addresses algorithmic ad delivery and lookalike audiences
Ensure listing-matching/recommendation algorithms do not systematically steer protected classes toward or away from certain listings
Apply the same standard to tenant-matching or screening-criteria tools that could function as a proxy for discriminatory advertising
items.penalties: HUD administrative complaints/charges, private lawsuits, civil penalties, and damages; HUD's 2019 charge against Facebook over ad-targeting tools is a relevant precedent for platform/vendor exposure
items.effective_or_amended: HUD FHEO Guidance on Advertising Through Digital Platforms, 2024
items.uncertainty: Primary source_url used is a HUD/DOJ joint statement summarizing 3604(c); the 2024 digital-advertising guidance PDF (in secondary_sources) is on the archives.hud.gov subdomain, still an official HUD source but not independently re-fetched in full this session.

how_to_comply.step: Build content-review or automated screening into listing/ad-creation tools to catch language or imagery that conveys a preference/limitation on a protected class before publication

If LOVELEEDAY builds or integrates digital ad-targeting for property clients, disable or restrict targeting parameters that exclude protected classes or their proxies (following the HUD v. Facebook precedent and 2024 digital-platform guidance)
Audit any listing-recommendation or matching algorithm for disparate steering effects on protected classes

items.attestation: No formal certificate; a fair-housing compliance review or documented ad-targeting restrictions is what a sophisticated property client or HUD investigation would look for
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY builds listing, advertising, tenant-matching/recommendation, or ad-targeting features used to advertise or match applicants to a dwelling
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's product is limited to internal operations (maintenance tickets, rent collection, accounting) with no advertising or applicant-matching feature
items.effort: medium — mostly product-design guardrails (content review, restricted targeting parameters) rather than a certification

items.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 — Free Baseline
items.citation: NIST CSWP 29, The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 (Feb. 2024)
items.applies_to_vendor: LOVELEEDAY can adopt NIST CSF 2.0 as a free, voluntary baseline to organize and communicate its cybersecurity program across all six industries it serves — CSF 2.0 is not a certification, but many buyers accept a CSF-organized security questionnaire response, and it maps cleanly to controls also required by SP 800-171/CMMC, the FTC Safeguards Rule, and SOC 2's Trust Services Criteria.
key_obligations: Organize the security program around CSF 2.0's six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover
Use the framework's Tiers to characterize the rigor of current cybersecurity risk-governance practices and Profiles to describe current vs. target state
No mandatory reporting or external audit — CSF 2.0 is self-implemented and voluntary unless a specific contract or other law separately requires it
items.penalties: None directly — voluntary framework, no enforcement mechanism of its own
items.effective_or_amended: CSF 2.0 released February 26, 2024

how_to_comply.step: Map LOVELEEDAY's existing security controls (from the SOC 2 / FTC Act reasonable-security program) to the CSF 2.0 six Functions to produce a Current Profile
Identify gaps against a Target Profile appropriate to the sensitivity of client data handled across the six served industries
Use the resulting CSF-organized documentation to answer client security questionnaires and RFPs at $0 marginal certification cost

items.attestation: No certificate — a CSF-mapped self-assessment/questionnaire response is the artifact buyers see
items.triggered_when: Any client across LOVELEEDAY's industries requests a structured description of LOVELEEDAY's cybersecurity risk-management program, or LOVELEEDAY wants a free baseline before investing in SOC 2/ISO 27001
items.not_triggered_when: Not applicable — free and voluntary for every LOVELEEDAY engagement; there's no scenario where adopting it is inappropriate
items.effort: low — free framework, self-implemented; the effort is in mapping existing controls, not in a new audit

items.title: Public-Records Exposure of Vendor Contracts and Data Held for Government Clients (general note; federal FAR analog)
items.citation: 48 CFR Subpart 24.2 (FAR Part 24, Protection of Privacy and Freedom of Information), 48 CFR 24.202–24.203
items.applies_to_vendor: General principle, illustrated by the federal FOIA/FAR framework: records a vendor submits to, or creates for, a government agency (contracts, pricing, technical proposals, and often correspondence) become agency records subject to public-records/open-records requests, unless a specific statutory exemption (e.g., trade secrets, confidential commercial/financial information) applies and the vendor has properly marked/asserted it.
key_obligations: Under the federal framework, a competitive proposal in the government's possession is not releasable under FOIA (48 CFR 24.202), but after award, released records are evaluated under FOIA exemptions (trade secrets, confidential commercial or financial information) — the vendor must affirmatively mark and assert confidentiality to preserve protection (48 CFR 24.203)

Every U.S. state has its own open/public-records law (state analogs to FOIA) governing records held by state and local government agencies, including vendor contracts, invoices, and often correspondence with vendors — LOVELEEDAY must assume anything it sends to a local-government client can become a public record unless the client's specific state law provides an exemption LOVELEEDAY has invoked

Contracts with local governments should include a provision requiring the agency to notify the vendor of a public-records request for the vendor's confidential/proprietary information before releasing it, where the applicable state records law allows
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Public-records exposure is about the vendor's own contract/technical/pricing information, not client end-user PII per se, but overly broad recordkeeping practices increase what becomes discoverable.
items.penalties: Varies by state; disclosure of unmarked confidential information via a state public-records request; the federal analog is enforced through FOIA litigation against the agency, not the contractor
items.uncertainty: This item is deliberately a general, cross-jurisdiction note, not a 50-state survey. The federal FAR/FOIA provisions cited are directly binding only on federal procurement, not the state/municipal contracts LOVELEEDAY actually signs; they are cited per the brief's instruction to describe the general pattern from one authoritative source, illustrating the same trade-secret/confidential-commercial-information logic most state open-records laws (each with its own citation) also use. Each specific state or municipal client's own open-records statute should be checked before relying on any exemption.

how_to_comply.step: Mark all technical, pricing, and proprietary submissions to government clients as 'Confidential — Trade Secret/Proprietary' and identify the specific exemption category being claimed (mirrors the FAR 24.203 approach), so the client's records officer knows the vendor's position before a request is decided

Negotiate a contract clause requiring the government client to notify LOVELEEDAY before releasing records LOVELEEDAY has marked confidential, so LOVELEEDAY can seek a state-law exemption or objection if applicable
Before signing with any specific local-government client, have counsel check that state's own public/open-records statute (each state differs) for the scope of vendor-record exemptions available

items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY submits contracts, technical proposals, pricing, or other records to a state or local government client, all of which are presumptively public records absent a specific, properly asserted exemption
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY works only with private-sector or non-FOIA-exempt-agency clients where state open-records law does not apply
items.effort: low — primarily a contract-drafting and document-marking discipline, not a technical or certification program

items.title: FERPA — "school official" exception letting a vendor handle education records without consent
items.applies_to_vendor: A school/LEA may disclose personally identifiable information (PII) from education records to LOVELEEDAY without parent/eligible-student consent only if LOVELEEDAY is treated as a 'school official' with a legitimate educational interest. That requires LOVELEEDAY to (1) perform an institutional service or function the school would otherwise use its own employees for, (2) be under the school's direct control regarding use and maintenance of the records, and (3) be bound by the redisclosure limits of 99.33(a) — no further disclosure without consent, use limited to the purpose disclosed.
key_obligations: Be designated a 'school official' by written agreement/contract with each school or LEA client (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B))
Accept the school's direct control over the use and maintenance of the education records disclosed
Do not redisclose PII from education records to any other party without the school's/parent's prior consent (34 CFR 99.33(a)(1))
Use the information only for the purpose for which it was disclosed (34 CFR 99.33(a)(2))
Support the school's own reasonable methods to limit access to only those records for which there is a legitimate educational interest (34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(ii))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Applies to 'education records' — records directly related to a student and maintained by an educational agency/institution or a party acting for it (34 CFR 99.3). No student-breach-notice mechanism to the Dept. of Education exists under FERPA itself.
items.penalties: No direct FERPA penalty runs against the vendor. FERPA's sole federal enforcement remedy is against the educational agency/institution: the Family Policy Compliance Office (now Student Privacy Policy Office) can move to withdraw federal funding for a policy or practice of FERPA violations (20 U.S.C. 1232g(b)(1)). Vendor-facing consequences (termination, liability) come from the school's own contract.
items.effective_or_amended: 2011 (34 CFR Part 99 last substantively amended)
items.uncertainty: FERPA regulations do not themselves specify the required form/content of the written designation — 'reasonable methods' and 'direct control' are undefined terms interpreted case-by-case; schools vary in how formal the contract language must be.

how_to_comply.step: Include a 'school official' designation clause in every school/LEA contract or data-privacy agreement, citing 34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B) and naming the specific institutional service performed
Contractually accept the school's direct control over use/maintenance of the records and agree not to redisclose PII without consent per 34 CFR 99.33(a)
Limit LOVELEEDAY staff access to education records to those with a legitimate need tied to the contracted service
Return or destroy education records at contract end per the school's own retention terms (FERPA sets no fixed number of days)

items.attestation: A signed data-privacy agreement/contract addendum containing the 34 CFR 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B) school-official language (often satisfied by signing the SDPC National Data Privacy Agreement — see us-sdpc-ndpa)
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY stores, processes, or otherwise has access to K-12 or higher-ed student education records on behalf of a school or LEA client
items.not_triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY provides infrastructure only (e.g., encrypted storage it cannot itself decrypt) with no access to identifiable student records, or the school never discloses education records to LOVELEEDAY at all
items.effort: low — the compliance mechanism is a contract clause (school-official designation + redisclosure limits), not a technical build; effort rises to medium if LOVELEEDAY must also build deletion/return-of-records workflows to match contract terms.

items.title: Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA)
items.applies_to_vendor: PPRA obligations run against the State/local educational agency (SEA/LEA) receiving ED funds, not directly against vendors. It requires parental notice/consent (or opt-out) before students take a survey, analysis, or evaluation funded by an ED program that touches one of eight protected areas (political beliefs, mental/psychological problems, sex behavior/attitudes, illegal/self-incriminating/demeaning behavior, critical appraisals of family members, privileged relationships, religious practices, or income beyond program-eligibility purposes), and gives parents rights around marketing surveys and inspection of instructional material. Where LOVELEEDAY builds or administers a survey/assessment tool, or a product that could be used to market to or collect information from students for non-educational purposes, the LEA's PPRA duties flow into the vendor contract.
key_obligations: Do not administer, or help administer, a covered survey touching one of PPRA's eight protected areas without the LEA first providing parental notice and obtaining consent (for federally funded surveys) or an opt-out opportunity
Do not use information collected through the LEA relationship to market products/services to students or their families without parental notice and opt-out rights
Support the LEA's obligation to let parents inspect instructional materials and surveys used in ED-funded programs
Flow PPRA notice/consent controls into the product if it administers surveys on the LEA's behalf
items.penalties: No FERPA/PPRA-style penalty is spelled out for a vendor directly; ED's enforcement mechanism (via the Student Privacy Policy Office, same office that handles FERPA complaints) runs against the LEA/SEA, with withdrawal of ED funding as the ultimate remedy.
items.effective_or_amended: 2002 (No Child Left Behind Act amendments)
items.uncertainty: ED's published PPRA guidance does not spell out specific vendor contract-clause language the way FERPA's 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B) does; the vendor obligation is inferred from the LEA's own duty flowing down through the services contract, not a PPRA provision naming vendors directly. Did not separately verify the full text of 34 CFR Part 98 section-by-section this session (relied on studentprivacy.ed.gov's summary, an official ED source).

how_to_comply.step: Identify whether the product administers surveys/assessments that could touch PPRA's eight protected areas
Build in a flag/workflow so the LEA can issue the required parental notice and consent/opt-out before a covered survey is administered
Contractually commit not to use LEA-sourced student data for marketing without the LEA's PPRA-compliant parental notice/opt-out process

items.attestation: No federal PPRA attestation form; LEAs typically add a PPRA-compliance representation/contract clause covering surveys and marketing use, often folded into the SDPC NDPA
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY's product administers or processes a survey/analysis/evaluation funded by an ED program that touches one of PPRA's eight protected areas, or the product is used to market to students/families using LEA-sourced data
items.not_triggered_when: The product does not administer surveys touching the eight protected areas and is never used for marketing purposes
items.effort: low — mainly a contractual pass-through of the LEA's own notice/consent duties; no PPRA-specific technical build unless the product itself runs covered surveys.

items.title: GovRAMP (formerly StateRAMP) Security Authorization
items.applies_to_vendor: A cloud service provider (SaaS/PaaS/IaaS) selling to a state or local government that has adopted GovRAMP/StateRAMP policy must obtain a GovRAMP security status (Authorized, Provisional, or In Process) commensurate with the data category, via a StateRAMP-approved Third Party Assessment Organization (3PAO).
key_obligations: Classify the cloud offering's data using the StateRAMP Data Classification Tool to determine required security category
Engage a StateRAMP-approved 3PAO to perform a full security assessment
Complete the System Security Plan (SR-SSP), Security Controls Template (SR-SCT), and Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M)
Obtain sponsorship/approval from a participating government's Authorizing Official for full Authorized status
Maintain continuous monitoring post-authorization
items.penalties: Loss of eligibility to sell/renew contracts with state and local governments that mandate GovRAMP status
items.effective_or_amended: Security Assessment Framework v4.0, February 2025
items.uncertainty: GovRAMP is a voluntary/state-adopted program, not a federal statute — applicability depends on which state/local government client requires it in its procurement policy; did not confirm which specific states currently mandate it.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm whether target state/local government clients require GovRAMP/StateRAMP status in their procurement rules
Use the StateRAMP Data Classification Tool to determine the applicable security category for the LOVELEEDAY product
Engage a StateRAMP-approved 3PAO and notify the GovRAMP PMO to move status to 'In Process'
Complete SR-SSP, SR-SCT, and POA&M documentation and pass the 3PAO assessment for Authorization

items.attestation: GovRAMP Authorized or Provisional status listing on the GovRAMP Authorized Vendors list
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY sells a cloud-hosted SaaS product directly to a state agency or local government that has adopted a GovRAMP/StateRAMP requirement in procurement policy
items.not_triggered_when: Client governments have no GovRAMP mandate, or LOVELEEDAY's product is on-premise / not a cloud service in scope
items.effort: high — 6–12 months average per govramp.org, requires a paid 3PAO assessment and ongoing continuous monitoring

items.title: Texas Risk and Authorization Management Program (TX-RAMP)
items.citation: Texas Government Code § 2054.0593; TX-RAMP Program Manual v3.1 (May 2025)
items.applies_to_vendor: A cloud computing service provider must obtain TX-RAMP certification before contracting to provide the service to a Texas state agency, institution of higher education, or public community college.
key_obligations: Determine certification Level (Level 1 for public/non-confidential/low-impact data; Level 2 for confidential/higher-impact data)
Submit assessment responses meeting Level 2 criteria, or submit evidence of an equivalent StateRAMP Category 2 or FedRAMP Moderate authorization
May obtain TX-RAMP Provisional Status, allowing a Texas agency to contract for up to 18 months while full certification is completed
Maintain certification through DIR's ongoing program requirements
items.penalties: A Texas state agency, university, or community college may not enter into or renew a contract for a cloud computing service that has not received TX-RAMP certification
items.effective_or_amended: Program Manual 3.1, per DIR May 2025 publication
items.uncertainty: This program legally binds only contracts with Texas state agencies/higher-ed/community colleges, not Texas municipalities generally; jurisdiction recorded as US per registry instruction though the program is Texas-specific.

how_to_comply.step: Confirm the Texas client is a state agency, public university, or community college (TX-RAMP's actual scope) rather than a city/county not covered by the statute
Submit a TX-RAMP request through DIR and select Level 1 or Level 2 based on data sensitivity
Complete the assessment (or provide existing StateRAMP Category 2 / FedRAMP Moderate authorization as equivalent evidence) or apply for Provisional Status to contract while certification is pending

items.attestation: TX-RAMP Certification (Level 1 or Level 2) or Provisional Status letter from Texas DIR
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY contracts to provide a cloud computing service to a Texas state agency, public university, or community college
items.not_triggered_when: The Texas client is a city, county, or school district not covered by Texas Government Code 2054.0593, or the product is not a 'cloud computing service' as DIR defines it
items.effort: medium — Level 1 is a self-attestation; Level 2 requires a more detailed assessment, though existing StateRAMP/FedRAMP work can be reused

items.title: AICPA SOC 2 — System and Organization Controls Report
items.citation: AICPA SOC 2 (based on the AICPA Trust Services Criteria); 2018 SOC 2 Description Criteria (with revised implementation guidance, 2022)
items.applies_to_vendor: LOVELEEDAY, as a service organization holding data for professional-services clients (accounting firms, law firms, etc.), can undergo an independent CPA-firm audit against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy) and receive a SOC 2 report, which is the standard attestation professional-services buyers request of a software vendor.
key_obligations: A SOC 2 Type I report evaluates the design of controls at a specific point in time; a SOC 2 Type II report evaluates operating effectiveness over an observation window, typically 3 to 12 months
The report is prepared by a licensed CPA firm (not AICPA itself) performing an attestation engagement under AICPA's SSAE standards, using the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria and Description Criteria
Only a CPA firm can issue the report; AICPA membership/licensure governs which firms may perform SOC engagements
items.penalties: Not a legal penalty regime — failure to obtain SOC 2 typically means loss of the sales opportunities/RFPs that require it, not a fine
items.effective_or_amended: 2018 SOC 2 Description Criteria with revised implementation guidance, 2022

how_to_comply.step: Complete a readiness assessment (gap analysis against the Trust Services Criteria, typically security at minimum) — can be self-performed or via a readiness consultant
Remediate control gaps (access control, change management, encryption, vendor management, incident response, logging) and document policies
Engage a licensed CPA firm to perform a SOC 2 Type I examination first (point-in-time design assessment) to validate control design
Operate the controls through a 3–12 month observation window, then have the CPA firm perform the SOC 2 Type II examination testing operating effectiveness

items.attestation: SOC 2 Type I or Type II report issued by a licensed CPA firm
items.triggered_when: A professional-services client (accounting firm, law firm, consultancy) or its own regulators/auditors requires evidence of independently audited security controls before buying or renewing LOVELEEDAY's software
items.not_triggered_when: Small/early clients who accept a security questionnaire or self-attestation instead of a formal report — common for early-stage vendors before their first SOC 2
items.effort: high — Type I typically takes a few months of control remediation plus the audit; Type II adds a multi-month observation window before the audit; ongoing annual renewal effort thereafter

items.title: ABA Model Rule 1.6(c) — Lawyer's Duty of Reasonable Efforts to Prevent Disclosure, as it Flows Down to Vendors
items.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.6(c) (and Comment); related Model Rule 5.3 (supervision of nonlawyer assistance)
items.applies_to_vendor: Model Rule 1.6(c) requires a lawyer to 'make reasonable efforts to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or unauthorized access to, information relating to the representation of a client.' Because law firms are LOVELEEDAY's client, this duty flows down through Model Rule 5.3 to any nonlawyer vendor a firm uses — meaning a law-firm client will conduct (and expects LOVELEEDAY to support) due diligence on LOVELEEDAY as its technology vendor before entrusting client data to LOVELEEDAY's platform.
key_obligations: Model Rule 1.6(c): a lawyer must make reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized disclosure of or access to client information — the standard is 'reasonable,' not a specific technical checklist

Model Rule 5.3 requires supervising lawyers to make reasonable efforts to ensure a nonlawyer vendor's conduct is compatible with the lawyer's professional obligations, driving law-firm vendor due-diligence questionnaires

ABA Formal Opinion 477 (cybersecurity duties for electronic client information) and related ethics opinions describe factors a lawyer should evaluate before selecting a vendor: where the data is stored, who owns/controls it, whether it is encrypted, and the ability to retrieve/delete it

On a breach, the lawyer has a duty under Model Rule 1.4 to notify affected clients — a LOVELEEDAY security incident affecting a law-firm client's data would trigger that client's own notification duty, so LOVELEEDAY needs a prompt incident-notification process to the firm
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Information relating to the representation' is broader than PII — it includes any information about a legal matter, not just personal data.
items.penalties: Not directly enforceable against LOVELEEDAY (the Model Rules bind lawyers, adopted state-by-state by each state's bar); practical consequence is loss of law-firm clients or contract liability if LOVELEEDAY fails the firm's vendor diligence
items.uncertainty: Model Rules are adopted (often with local variations) by each state's bar, not directly binding in their ABA form; a specific law-firm client's home-state version of Rule 1.6(c)/5.3 could differ slightly.

how_to_comply.step: Maintain data location/ownership/encryption/deletion documentation (where data is stored, who controls it, how it's encrypted, how the firm can retrieve or purge it on termination) to answer law-firm vendor due-diligence questionnaires built around ABA Formal Opinion 477 factors
Build and commit to a prompt security-incident notification process to law-firm clients, supporting their Model Rule 1.4 client-notification duty
Offer a data-processing/confidentiality addendum in the LOVELEEDAY contract that mirrors Rule 1.6(c)'s reasonable-efforts standard (encryption, access control, staff confidentiality obligations)

items.attestation: No formal certificate; a completed vendor-security questionnaire and a signed confidentiality/data-processing addendum are what a law firm will actually request
items.triggered_when: LOVELEEDAY holds or processes 'information relating to the representation' for a law-firm client (documents, case data, communications)
items.not_triggered_when: The professional-services client is not a law firm (e.g., an accounting or consulting firm), where different professional-conduct rules apply instead
items.effort: low-medium — mostly documentation and contract-addendum work built on top of the general security program already required

items.title: ISO/IEC 27001 — Information Security Management System Certification
items.applies_to_vendor: LOVELEEDAY can implement an Information Security Management System (ISMS) conforming to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and obtain third-party certification from an accredited certification body, which is a cross-industry, internationally recognized way to demonstrate systematic security management to any client across all six of LOVELEEDAY's serviced industries.
key_obligations: Establish, implement, maintain, and continually improve an ISMS addressing organizational context, leadership commitment, risk assessment and treatment, and the Annex A control set
Undergo a two-stage external audit (Stage 1 documentation review, Stage 2 implementation audit) by an accredited certification body to obtain initial certification
Maintain the ISMS through annual surveillance audits and full recertification (typically every 3 years)
items.penalties: Not a legal penalty regime — loss of certification for noncompliance, and loss of sales opportunities requiring it
items.effective_or_amended: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (latest edition)

how_to_comply.step: Define the ISMS scope (which systems/data/offices are in-scope) and perform a risk assessment against ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 6 and the Annex A control set
Implement required controls, policies, and a Statement of Applicability documenting which Annex A controls apply and why
Engage an accredited certification body for the Stage 1/Stage 2 audit; maintain via annual surveillance audits

items.attestation: ISO/IEC 27001 certificate issued by an accredited certification body
items.triggered_when: A client in any LOVELEEDAY-served industry requires internationally recognized, independently certified security-management evidence (common in cross-border, enterprise, or government-adjacent procurement)
items.not_triggered_when: SOC 2 alone satisfies the client's requirement (common for U.S.-only buyers) — ISO 27001 and SOC 2 overlap substantially but are not identical; many small U.S. vendors start with SOC 2 and add ISO 27001 later for international/enterprise deals
items.effort: high — full ISMS build-out and external certification audit; similar or greater effort than SOC 2, with recurring annual surveillance

items.title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 — Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) scope and hosted/tokenized payment page reduction
items.citation: PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) v4.0.1, PCI Security Standards Council; SAQ A, SAQ A-EP, SAQ D (Merchant and Service Provider)
items.applies_to_vendor: PCI DSS applies to any entity that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, or that could impact the security of the cardholder data environment (CDE) — including a software vendor whose code runs on a client's payment page. If LOVELEEDAY's software ever touches cardholder data directly, LOVELEEDAY itself becomes a PCI DSS 'service provider' subject to the full SAQ D-SP / QSA-assessed requirements. If LOVELEEDAY instead architects payments through a fully hosted or tokenized third-party checkout (e.g., a redirect or an iframe/drop-in widget where no LOVELEEDAY-served code touches card fields), both LOVELEEDAY and the hospitality/retail/nonprofit client stay eligible for the lightest self-assessment, SAQ A (only ~24 requirements), and LOVELEEDAY can often stay entirely out of PCI scope.
key_obligations: Determine whether any LOVELEEDAY-built or LOVELEEDAY-hosted code touches cardholder data or the payment page at all

If touching card data: implement the full PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement set and complete the applicable SAQ (or full Report on Compliance if a large service provider) with an Attestation of Compliance (AOC)

If NOT touching card data: confirm and document the eligibility criteria for SAQ A — payment fully outsourced to a PCI DSS compliant third-party service provider (TPSP), no electronic storage/processing/transmission of account data on LOVELEEDAY or client systems, and (for e-commerce) every element of the payment page originates directly from the compliant TPSP
Review the TPSP's own PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance annually
Reassess PCI scope whenever the payment integration architecture changes (e.g., adding any client-side script that touches the card fields moves the merchant from SAQ A to SAQ A-EP or higher)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Account data' = cardholder data (PAN, cardholder name, expiration date, service code) plus sensitive authentication data (full track data, CVV, PINs/PIN blocks); PCI DSS is a payment-brand contractual standard, not a government regulation, so there is no 'personal info' statutory definition — scope is defined by the PCI SSC's own Applicability Information.
items.penalties: Not government-imposed; enforcement runs through the card networks/acquiring banks via merchant/processor agreements — fines, increased transaction fees, or loss of card-acceptance privileges for non-compliance or after a breach involving unsecured cardholder data.
items.effective_or_amended: PCI DSS v4.0.1 (June 2024); SAQs for v4.0.1 published October 2024; PCI DSS v4.0 retired December 31, 2024

items.title: Data Breach Notification Act of 2018
items.applies_to_vendor: A 'third-party agent' (an entity contracted to maintain, store, process, or otherwise access sensitive personally identifying information for a covered entity) that experiences a breach must notify the covered entity as expeditiously as possible and without unreasonable delay, no later than 10 days following determination of the breach or reason to believe it occurred (§8-38-8). The third-party agent must cooperate with the covered entity by providing information in its possession so the covered entity can meet its own notice duties; the parties may contract for the third-party agent to handle notifications directly. Failure to inform the covered entity subjects the third-party agent to the chapter's fines and penalties (§8-38-9(b)(4)).
key_obligations: Third-party agent must notify covered entity of a breach within 10 days of determination (§8-38-8)
Covered entity must notify affected individuals within 45 days of receiving notice from a third-party agent or of its own determination (§8-38-5(b))
Covered entity must notify the Attorney General within 45 days if the breach affects more than 1,000 individuals (§8-38-6)
Covered entity and third-party agent must implement and maintain reasonable security measures (§8-38-3)
Covered entity must notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies if the breach affects more than 1,000 individuals at a single time (§8-38-7)
Covered entity/third-party agent must take reasonable measures to dispose of records containing sensitive PII when no longer needed (§8-38-10)
items.notice_deadline: "as expeditiously as possible and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 10 days following the determination of the breach of security" (third-party agent to covered entity, §8-38-8); "as expeditiously as possible and without unreasonable delay... within 45 days" (covered entity to individuals and Attorney General, §§8-38-5(b), 8-38-6(a))
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General notice required if the number of individuals to be notified exceeds 1,000; written notice within 45 days (§8-38-6)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Sensitive personally identifying information" = first name/initial + last name plus one of: non-truncated SSN/tax ID; non-truncated driver's license/state ID/passport/military ID number; financial account number + security/access code or password; medical history/treatment/diagnosis info; health insurance policy/subscriber ID; or username/email + password/security question-answer permitting account access (§8-38-2(6))
items.penalties: Enforced exclusively by the Attorney General as an unlawful trade practice under the Alabama Deceptive Trade Practices Act; no private right of action; civil penalties up to $500,000 per breach for knowing violations, plus up to $5,000 per day for continued noncompliance (§8-38-9)
