items.title: Alabama Personal Data Protection Act (APDPA)
items.citation: HB 351, 2026 Regular Session (enrolled act, to be codified in the Code of Alabama 1975)
items.applies_to_vendor: Defines 'processor' as an individual or legal entity that processes personal data on behalf of a controller. Requires a binding contract between controller and processor setting out processing instructions, nature, purpose, duration, and type of data. The processor must: ensure persons processing data are subject to confidentiality; assist the controller in meeting security and consumer-rights obligations; delete or return data to the controller at the end of services unless retention is legally required; make information available to demonstrate compliance on reasonable request; and require subcontractors to meet the same obligations (Section 9, deidentified-data cross-reference at Section 2(10)(c)).
key_obligations: Applies to persons conducting business in Alabama or producing products/services targeted to Alabama residents who (1) control or process the personal data of 25,000+ consumers, excluding data controlled/processed solely for completing a payment transaction, or (2) derive more than 25% of gross revenue from the sale of personal data (Section 3)

Grants consumers rights to access, correct, delete, and obtain a portable copy of personal data, and to opt out of sale of personal data and certain targeted advertising/profiling (Section 1 preamble)

Exempts political subdivisions, certain boards/authorities, two- and four-year institutions of higher education, national securities associations, GLBA-governed financial institutions, and HIPAA covered entities/business associates, among others (Section 4)

Enforced exclusively by the Attorney General; must issue a notice of violation and allow a 45-day cure period before suing; court may assess a civil penalty of not more than $15,000 per violation if uncured (Section 11)
No private right of action referenced in the enrolled text
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General enforcement only; a 45-day cure period after a notice of violation is required before an enforcement action may be brought (Section 11(b))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Sensitive data" includes racial/ethnic origin, religious beliefs, mental/physical health condition or diagnosis, sex life/sexual orientation, citizenship/immigration status, genetic or biometric data used to uniquely identify an individual, personal data collected from a known child, and precise geolocation data (Section 2(21))
items.penalties: Civil penalty of not more than $15,000 per violation, assessed by a court following an Attorney General enforcement action after an uncured 45-day notice of violation (Section 11(b)(2))
items.effective_or_amended: Signed by the Governor April 17, 2026 (unanimous passage: House 104-0, Senate 34-0); effective May 1, 2027 (Section 12)

items.citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 4-110-101 et seq. (enacted as Act 1526 of 2005, SB1167)

items.title: Student Data Vendor Security Act
items.citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 6-18-2501 et seq. (Act 754 of 2023, HB1757)
items.applies_to_vendor: Each local education agency (LEA) must ensure that contracts disclosing or making available student personally identifiable information (PII) to vendors — including school service contract providers, school service on-demand providers, and subcontractors — include express provisions safeguarding the privacy and security of student PII (§6-18-2504(a)). Contracts with school service contract providers entered into or renewed on/after the effective date must, at minimum, require the provider to comply with §§6-18-2505 and 6-18-2507. If a provider commits a material breach involving misuse or unauthorized release of student PII, the LEA must investigate, give the provider an opportunity to respond, obtain governing-body direction, and determine whether to terminate the contract (§6-18-2504(b)).
key_obligations: LEA must maintain a list of school service contract providers and update it at the beginning and mid-point of each school year (§6-18-2504(b)(1))
LEA must provide the list and a copy of each contract to a parent on request
Vendor contracts must comply with §§6-18-2505 and 6-18-2507 (vendor obligations)
LEA shall not enter/renew a contract with a provider that refuses these terms or has substantially failed to comply
LEA must maintain a similar list of school service on-demand providers and assist parents in obtaining the on-demand provider's data privacy policy on request
Material breach involving misuse/unauthorized release of student PII triggers an investigation, response opportunity, and termination/continuation determination
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Student personally identifiable information" = information that, alone or in combination, personally identifies an individual student or the student's parent/family and is collected, maintained, generated, or inferred by a public education entity (directly or through a school service), a school service contract provider, or a school service on-demand provider; excludes deidentified data (§6-18-2503(11))

A third party maintaining data for another must notify the owner/licensee 'as soon as practicable' and cooperate with the investigation (§18-552(C))

items.penalties: Violation is an unlawful practice enforceable exclusively by the Attorney General; civil penalty capped at the lesser of $10,000 per affected individual or the total economic loss sustained by affected individuals, with an overall cap of $500,000 per breach or related series of breaches; restitution for affected individuals may also be recovered

key_obligations: No targeted advertising to students based on covered information
No amassing a student profile except in furtherance of school purposes
No sale or rental of student information

items.title: Customer Records — breach of security (California data breach notification law)

Notice must use a titled 'Notice of Data Breach' format with specified headings, 10-point minimum font, and plain language
A copy of the notice must be provided to the Attorney General if a single breach requires notifying more than 500 California residents
Substitute notice is permitted above specified cost/scale thresholds

items.title: California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (CCPA/CPRA)
items.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100 et seq. (definitions and thresholds at § 1798.140)
items.applies_to_vendor: A 'service provider' processes personal information on behalf of a business under a written contract that must prohibit selling/sharing the data, restrict its retention/use/disclosure to specified business purposes, and prohibit combining it with other sources except as permitted. A 'contractor' (a business's counterparty receiving personal information for business purposes) is bound by materially identical contractual restrictions. Businesses must ensure service providers/contractors have equivalent privacy obligations, can monitor their compliance, halt unauthorized use, and be notified if the service provider/contractor is unable to comply (§1798.100).
key_obligations: Applies to a 'business' meeting at least one threshold: annual gross revenue exceeding $25,000,000; annually buys/sells/shares personal information of 100,000+ consumers or households; or derives 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing consumers' personal information (§1798.140)
Grants consumers rights to know, delete, correct, and opt out of the sale/sharing of personal information and of certain automated decision-making
Requires a written contract between business and service provider/contractor containing specified use and retention restrictions
Businesses must implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the information
Enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency and the Attorney General
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Broad 'personal information' definition; a separate, narrower category of 'sensitive personal information' carries additional disclosure and opt-out-of-use rights
items.effective_or_amended: CCPA effective January 1, 2020; amended by the CPRA (Proposition 24), with CPRA amendments effective January 1, 2023

No use of information to amass a profile about a pupil except in furtherance of K-12 school purposes
No sale of student/covered information

Deletion of covered information within 60 days of a qualifying deletion request
Disclosures permitted for legitimate educational purposes, legal compliance, court order, safety/security, and to service providers under contractual use restrictions
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Covered information" includes personally identifiable information created by students/parents/school staff or gathered by the operator: names, addresses, grades, test results, discipline records, medical/health records, biometric data, and geolocation information, among other data elements

Requires a binding processing agreement between controller and processor
Requires controllers to conduct data protection assessments for higher-risk processing and to obtain consent before processing certain sensitive personal data
Final rules, including universal opt-out mechanism specifications required by §6-1-1313(2), were filed with the Secretary of State March 15, 2023
Enforced by the Colorado Attorney General, which began CPA enforcement (education-focused notice letters) on July 12, 2023

items.title: Student Data Transparency and Security Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to 'school service contract providers' (vendors under a formal, negotiated contract with a public education entity to provide a school service) and 'school service on-demand providers.' The Colorado Department of Education must ensure that contracts entered into or renewed with a school service contract provider require the provider, at minimum, to comply with §§22-16-108 to 22-16-110. If a contract provider commits a material breach involving misuse or unauthorized release of student personally identifiable information, the department must determine whether to terminate the contract following a public-hearing process that includes an opportunity for the provider to respond. The department may not enter into or renew a contract with a provider that refuses these terms or has substantially failed to comply (§22-16-105).
key_obligations: Department must publish and maintain a list of all vendors/entities holding student personally identifiable information and a copy of each contract or agreement (§22-16-105(4))
Vendor contracts must, at minimum, require compliance with §§22-16-108 to 22-16-110
Department shall not sell, trade, gift, or monetize student personally identifiable information for commercial use or investment interests (§22-16-105(3)(d))

Department shall not transfer student personally identifiable information out of state except under enumerated exceptions (e.g., student transfer, out-of-state enrollment, required program participation, migrant classification, specified vendor/researcher contracts, legal process)
Department's data security guidance for local education providers must address security-breach planning, notice, and procedures, and data retention/destruction (§22-16-106)
Material breach by a contract provider triggers an investigation, a response opportunity, and a termination/continuation determination by the department in accordance with state board policy
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Student personally identifiable information" = information that, alone or in combination, personally identifies an individual student or the student's parent/family and is collected, maintained, generated, or inferred by a public education entity, directly or through a school service, or by a school service contract provider or school service on-demand provider (§22-16-103(13))
items.effective_or_amended: 2016 (HB16-1423), effective August 10, 2016
items.uncertainty: No separate statutory civil penalty was located in the sections reviewed (§§22-16-101 to 22-16-106); contract termination by the department is the enforcement mechanism described in the text reviewed.

items.title: Breach of security re computerized data containing personal information
items.applies_to_vendor: Any person that maintains computerized data that includes personal information that the person does not own shall notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of the security of the data immediately following its discovery, if the personal information of a Connecticut resident was breached or is reasonably believed to have been breached (§36a-701b(c)).
key_obligations: Owner/licensee must notify affected Connecticut residents without unreasonable delay, not later than 60 days after discovery of the breach, unless a shorter time is required under federal law (§36a-701b(b)(1))

Owner/licensee must notify the Attorney General no later than the time notice is provided to residents — required whenever resident notice is required, with no separate numeric affected-persons threshold (§36a-701b(b)(2)(A))

Owner/licensee must offer affected residents free identity theft prevention services and, if applicable, identity theft mitigation services for not less than two years, where SSN or certain other listed data elements were breached (§36a-701b(b)(2)(B))
Notice may be delayed for a reasonable period if a law enforcement agency determines it would impede a criminal investigation and requests the delay (§36a-701b(d))

Failure to comply constitutes an unfair trade practice under CUTPA (§42-110b), enforced exclusively by the Attorney General; civil penalties may be deposited into the state's privacy protection guaranty and enforcement account (§36a-701b(j)-(k))
items.notice_deadline: "without unreasonable delay but not later than sixty days after the discovery of such breach" (owner/licensee to residents, §36a-701b(b)(1)); "immediately following its discovery" (non-owning maintainer/vendor to owner/licensee, §36a-701b(c))
items.regulator_notice: Attorney General must be notified no later than when resident notice is provided; no numeric affected-persons threshold in the statutory text reviewed
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Includes SSN, taxpayer ID, IRS identity-protection PIN, driver's license/state ID/passport/military ID, credit/debit card number, financial account number + required security/access code or password, medical history/treatment/diagnosis information, health insurance policy/subscriber ID, biometric information, precise geolocation data (as defined in §42-515), and username/email address + password or security question/answer
items.penalties: Failure to comply is an unfair trade practice under CUTPA (Conn. Gen. Stat. §42-110b), enforced exclusively by the Attorney General; civil penalties collected may be deposited into the privacy protection guaranty and enforcement account
items.effective_or_amended: Originally P.A. 05-148; most recently amended by P.A. 23-98, §4 (per the statute's history note)

items.title: Connecticut Data Privacy Act (CTDPA)
items.citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-515 to 42-525 (Chapter 743jj, Part I — Consumer Data Privacy and Online Monitoring)
items.applies_to_vendor: A 'processor' shall adhere to the instructions of a controller and shall assist the controller in meeting its obligations under §§42-515 to 42-525, including: fulfilling consumer-rights requests; assisting with security-of-processing obligations and breach-of-security notification (referencing §36a-701b) for the processor's own systems; and providing information to enable the controller to conduct data protection assessments. The controller-processor contract must be binding, clearly set forth processing instructions, the nature/purpose of processing, the type of data, and the duration of processing, and must require the processor to: keep personal data confidential; delete or return all personal data to the controller at the end of services unless retention is required by law; make information available on reasonable request to demonstrate compliance; engage subcontractors only under a written contract requiring them to meet the processor's obligations (after giving the controller an opportunity to object); and cooperate with reasonable compliance assessments (§42-521).
key_obligations: Applies to persons that conduct business in Connecticut or produce products/services targeted to Connecticut residents and meet statutory thresholds (definitions at §42-515)

Exempts, among others, state/local government bodies, entities processing consumer health data under contract with such bodies, nonprofit organizations, institutions of higher education, certain national securities associations, GLBA-governed financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities/business associates, tribal nation government organizations, and regulated air carriers (§42-517)
Requires controllers to conduct data protection assessments for higher-risk processing and disclose them to the Attorney General on request (§42-522)
Enforced by the Attorney General with a notice-of-violation and cure-period process, reporting requirement, and penalty provision (§42-525)
Later-added provisions in the same chapter cover consumer health data privacy (§42-526) and minors'/social media platform data (§42-528)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Definitions include detailed treatment of biometric data, consent (with dark-pattern and passive-interaction exclusions), child (per COPPA), business associate (per HIPAA), and abortion as a defined term relevant to sensitive/consumer health data
items.effective_or_amended: Enacted 2022; effective July 1, 2023; the chapter has since been amended to add consumer health data privacy and minors'/social-media provisions
items.uncertainty: The specific penalty amount under §42-525's Attorney General enforcement/cure-period process was not extracted in the fetched excerpt this session (only the section heading confirming a cure period, report, and penalty exists).

items.title: Student Data Privacy Act (as amended)
items.applies_to_vendor: Defines a 'contractor' as an operator or consultant in possession of, or with access to, student information/records/generated content as a result of a contract with a local or regional board of education. On and after July 1, 2018, a board of education must enter into a written contract with a contractor any time it shares or provides access to student information, student records, or student-generated content. Each such contract must include at least 10 enumerated provisions, including: a statement that the data is not the property of the contractor; deletion-request procedures; a use limitation to purposes authorized by the contract; correction procedures for erroneous information; security/confidentiality obligations; a procedure for the contractor to notify the board of an unauthorized release, disclosure, or acquisition of student data per §10-234dd; a limitation on retaining data after contract expiration; a FERPA-compliance statement; Connecticut choice-of-law; and severability (§10-234bb(a)).
key_obligations: Written contract required before a board of education shares or provides a contractor access to student information/records/generated content (on/after July 1, 2018)
Contract must state the data is not the property of or under the contractor's control
Contract must describe deletion-request procedures, with limited exceptions for legally required retention and disaster-recovery copies
Contract must limit the contractor's use of student data to purposes authorized by the contract
Contract must describe procedures for reviewing and correcting erroneous personally identifiable information
Contract must require the contractor to take actions ensuring the security and confidentiality of student data
Contract must describe the contractor's procedure for notifying the board of an unauthorized release/disclosure/acquisition of student data (per §10-234dd)
Contract must bar retention of student data after contract expiration (subject to limited student/parent-initiated exceptions) and require FERPA compliance
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Student information" is broadly defined to include information in a student's records or email account, name, address, phone number, date of birth, email address, discipline records, test results, grades, evaluations, criminal records, medical/health records, SSN, biometric information, disabilities, socioeconomic information, food purchases, political/religious affiliations, text messages, documents, student identifiers, search activity, photographs, voice recordings, survey responses, or behavioral assessments
items.effective_or_amended: Originally enacted as P.A. 16-189 (2016); amended by P.A. 17-200 and P.A. 18-125; the written-contract requirement is effective on and after July 1, 2018
items.uncertainty: No standalone statutory penalty for noncompliance was located in the sections reviewed (§§10-234aa, 10-234bb); enforcement is structured through the required board-contractor contract terms rather than a separate civil-penalty provision in the text reviewed.

items.title: Consumer Security Breach Notification Act
items.citation: D.C. Code § 28-3851 et seq. (Title 28, Chapter 38, Subchapter II)
items.applies_to_vendor: A person or entity that maintains, handles, or otherwise possesses personal information that it does not own or license (a vendor/service provider) must notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of the security of the system in the most expedient time possible following discovery, and must cooperate with the owner/licensee, including informing them of the date/nature of the breach and any remedial steps taken. The data owner then bears responsibility for notifying affected DC residents.
key_obligations: Third party/vendor holding data it does not own must notify the data owner or licensee of a breach 'in the most expedient time possible' following discovery, and must cooperate with the owner/licensee on remediation (D.C. Code § 28-3852(b))
Data owner/licensee must notify affected DC residents in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay
If a breach affects 50 or more DC residents, the entity must notify the DC Attorney General in the most expedient manner possible, and no later than when resident notice is given
A waiver of the subchapter's protections is void and unenforceable
items.notice_deadline: "the most expedient time possible following discovery" (vendor-to-owner notice); "most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" (owner-to-resident notice) — statute does not convert this to a fixed number of days
items.regulator_notice: DC Attorney General must be notified if a breach affects 50 or more District residents, in the most expedient manner possible and no later than when resident notice is provided (D.C. Code § 28-3852)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Definition is in D.C. Code § 28-3851(3), cross-referenced by § 28-3852; not independently re-fetched this session beyond what secondary summaries describe (SSN, driver's license/ID numbers, financial account numbers, and by 2020 amendment also biometric data, health/health-insurance information, taxpayer ID, and username/email plus password) — recommend a direct fetch of § 28-3851 to confirm exact wording.
items.penalties: The DC Attorney General may seek injunctive relief and restitution and recover a civil penalty not to exceed $100 per violation, plus costs and attorneys' fees (D.C. Code § 28-3853); a violation is also an unfair or deceptive trade practice under § 28-3904(kk); a DC resident injured by a violation has a private right of action for actual damages (excluding dignitary/pain-and-suffering damages), costs and attorneys' fees.
items.uncertainty: Fetched § 28-3852 directly from code.dccouncil.gov (official) this session and it supports the vendor-notification and AG-threshold language quoted above. items.title: Protecting Students Digital Privacy Act of 2016
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds 'operators' of internet websites, online services, online applications, or mobile applications used primarily for K-12 school purposes and designed/marketed for that purpose. Operators must implement reasonable security, acknowledge LEA control of student data, delete personally identifiable student information within a reasonable time after termination of services, and notify the LEA of unauthorized access. Operators are barred from selling/renting/trading student data, targeted advertising using student data, or building non-educational profiles of students.
key_obligations: Operators must 'implement and maintain reasonable security policies and procedures appropriate to the nature of the personally identifiable student information'
Student information 'is under the control of the LEA' — operators may not treat it as their own
Operators must 'delete personally identifiable student information...within a reasonable period of time after termination or completion of services'
Operators must notify the LEA of 'unauthorized access to personally identifiable student information'
Operators may not 'sell, rent, or trade any personally identifiable student information' except in a business acquisition or with verified parental consent for specific educational purposes
Operators may not engage in targeted advertising based on information acquired through a student's use of the service
Operators may not use student data to build a non-educational profile of a student or group of students

items.title: Computer Security Breaches
items.applies_to_vendor: A person that maintains computerized data that includes personal information that the person does not own shall give notice to and cooperate with the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of security immediately following determination of the breach of security (§12B-102).
key_obligations: Owner/licensee must provide notice to affected Delaware residents without unreasonable delay, but not later than 60 days after determination of the breach of security, subject to exceptions for federal-law compliance and law-enforcement investigations (§12B-102)
Owner/licensee must notify the Attorney General, no later than the time notice is provided to the resident, if the affected number of Delaware residents to be notified exceeds 500
Persons owning/licensing computerized data with personal information about Delaware residents must implement reasonable security procedures

items.title: Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act (DPDPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: Processors must adhere to controller instructions and assist the controller in meeting its obligations, including: implementing appropriate technical/organizational safeguards to help fulfill consumer-rights requests; assisting with data security and breach-notification responsibilities; and providing information enabling the controller to conduct data protection assessments. Controller-processor relationships must be governed by a binding contract with clear processing instructions that requires the processor to: ensure each person processing personal data is subject to a duty of confidentiality; delete or return data upon the controller's direction at the end of services (unless retention is legally required); provide information on reasonable request to demonstrate compliance; and require subcontractors to meet the same processor obligations.
key_obligations: Until January 1, 2027: applies to entities controlling/processing the personal data of 35,000 or more consumers, or of 10,000 or more consumers while deriving 20% or more of gross revenue from the sale of personal data

From January 1, 2027: thresholds change to 10,000 or more consumers, or 5,000 or more consumers while deriving 20% or more of revenue from sale, and the applicability is expanded to include third parties acquiring personal data from controllers
Data protection assessments required for higher-risk processing activities created after July 1, 2025
Requires a binding controller-processor contract meeting the statutory content requirements
items.effective_or_amended: Original enactment 84 Del. Laws, c. 197 (most provisions effective immediately); expanded requirements effective January 1, 2027 per 85 Del. Laws, c. 463; data protection assessment requirement applies to processing activities created after July 1, 2025

items.title: Student Data Privacy Protection Act

Operators must implement security measures complying with the Delaware Department of Technology and Information's Cloud Hosting Policy, and must delete a student's data within a reasonable timeframe not to exceed 45 calendar days when requested by a school district (§8104A, Operator duties). Operators may not engage in targeted advertising based on student data, may not create student profiles outside K-12 purposes, and may not sell student information (§8105A, Operator prohibited activities). Data disclosures are limited to legal-compliance, judicial-process, security-protection, and service-provider scenarios under strict contractual restrictions.
key_obligations: No targeted advertising based on student data
No creation of comprehensive student profiles/dossiers outside K-12 educational purposes
No sale of student information
Security measures must comply with the Department of Technology and Information's Cloud Hosting Policy
Delete a student's data within a reasonable timeframe not to exceed 45 calendar days of a school-district request
Enforced by the Consumer Protection Unit of the Delaware Department of Justice under Title 29, Chapter 25's consumer protection provisions
items.effective_or_amended: Per 80 Del. Laws, c. 149

items.title: Florida Information Protection Act of 2014 (FIPA)
items.applies_to_vendor: A 'third-party agent' — an entity contracted to maintain, store, or process personal information on behalf of a covered entity or governmental entity — must notify the covered entity of a breach as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 10 days following determination of the breach (or reason to believe the breach occurred). The covered entity then bears the duty to notify affected individuals and, above a threshold, the Florida Department of Legal Affairs (Attorney General).
key_obligations: Third-party agent must notify the covered entity 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 10 days following the determination of the breach'

Covered entity must notify the Florida Department of Legal Affairs when a breach affects 500 or more individuals in Florida, 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 30 days after the determination of the breach'
A violation is treated as an unfair or deceptive trade practice enforceable by the department under § 501.207
Civil penalties for late/failed notice: $1,000/day for the first 30 days, then $50,000 per 30-day period thereafter, up to $500,000 total, per breach (not per individual)
items.notice_deadline: third-party agent to covered entity: 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 10 days following the determination of the breach'; covered entity to Dept. of Legal Affairs: 'as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than 30 days after the determination of the breach'
items.regulator_notice: Florida Department of Legal Affairs (Attorney General) must be notified when a breach affects 500 or more Florida individuals
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Includes SSN; government-issued ID numbers; financial account/card numbers with security codes; medical history/treatment information; health insurance policy numbers; biometric data; geolocation information — each combined with name, or username/email plus password.
items.penalties: Civil penalty of $1,000 per day for the first 30 days, then $50,000 per 30-day period (or portion) thereafter, capped at $500,000 for violations continuing beyond 180 days; penalty applies per breach, not per individual
items.effective_or_amended: 2023 (last amended by s. 25, ch. 2023-201; originally enacted 2014)

items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to 'controllers' that do business in Florida, collect personal data of Florida consumers (or have it collected on their behalf), determine the purposes/means of processing, and (a) have global gross annual revenue exceeding $1 billion, AND (b) meet at least one of: derive 50%+ of global gross annual revenue from online advertising sales, operate a smart-speaker/voice-assistant service, or operate an app store/digital distribution platform offering 250,000+ applications. items.title: Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)

The entity must publish a written retention schedule and destruction guidelines, may not sell/lease/trade/profit from the data, and may only disclose it with consent, to complete a subject-requested transaction, as required by law, or pursuant to a valid warrant/subpoena.

items.applies_to_vendor: Any "information holder" that maintains computerized data including personally identifiable information it does not own shall notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach of security of the data as soon as reasonably practicable following discovery, if the information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person (KRS 365.732(3)).
key_obligations: An information holder must disclose any breach of the security of the system to any affected Kentucky resident, following discovery or notification, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay (KRS 365.732(2))
An information holder maintaining data it does not own must notify the owner or licensee of the information of any breach as soon as reasonably practicable following discovery (KRS 365.732(3))
Notification may be delayed if a law enforcement agency determines it would impede a criminal investigation; notice must be made promptly after the agency clears it (KRS 365.732(4))

Notice may be written, electronic (per 15 U.S.C. §7001), or substitute notice if cost would exceed $250,000, the affected class exceeds 500,000 persons, or the holder lacks sufficient contact information (KRS 365.732(5))

If a breach requires notification of more than 1,000 persons at one time, the information holder must also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies and credit bureaus without unreasonable delay (KRS 365.732(7))
GLBA- and HIPAA-regulated entities, and Kentucky state/local government agencies, are exempt from this section (KRS 365.732(8))
items.notice_deadline: "the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" (§2); "as soon as reasonably practicable following discovery" for the vendor-to-owner duty (§3) -- no fixed day count
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Personally identifiable information" is first name/initial + last name combined with SSN, driver's license number, or account/credit/debit card number with any required security/access code -- unredacted. "Breach of the security of the system" requires the unauthorized acquisition of unencrypted, unredacted data that actually causes, or is reasonably believed will cause, identity theft or fraud (KRS 365.732(1)).
items.effective_or_amended: Effective July 15, 2014 (Created 2014 Ky. Acts ch. 84, sec. 1)

items.title: Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to a "processor" that processes personal data on behalf of a controller; the processor must adhere to the controller's instructions and assist with consumer-rights compliance, security/breach obligations, and data protection assessments, under a binding contract (KRS 367.3619).
key_obligations: Applies to persons conducting business in Kentucky, or producing products/services targeted to KY residents, that during a calendar year control or process personal data of at least 100,000 consumers, or at least 25,000 consumers while deriving over 50% of gross revenue from selling personal data (KRS 367.3613(1))

Exempts state/local government, GLBA-regulated financial institutions, HIPAA covered entities/business associates, nonprofits, higher-ed institutions, and certain other narrow categories (KRS 367.3613(2))

Processor must assist controller in responding to consumer-rights requests, meeting security and breach-notification obligations (which route through KRS 365.732), and completing data protection assessments (KRS 367.3619(1))

A binding contract between controller and processor must set out processing instructions, nature/purpose/duration of processing, and require confidentiality, deletion/return of data at contract end, compliance demonstration, cooperation with assessments, and flow-down obligations to subcontractors (KRS 367.3619(2))

The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and must give 30 days' written notice of an alleged violation before suing; if cured within 30 days with a written statement of cure, no damages action may be brought (KRS 367.3627(1)-(2))
If violations continue after the cure period, the AG may seek damages of up to $7,500 per continued violation; the Act creates no private right of action (KRS 367.3627(3)-(4))
items.regulator_notice: 30 days' written notice from the Attorney General identifying the specific provisions alleged to be violated, before any enforcement action; curable within that 30-day window (KRS 367.3627(2))
items.penalties: Up to $7,500 per continued violation after the cure period, plus recovery of the AG's reasonable investigation/litigation expenses, court costs, and attorney's fees (KRS 367.3627(3), (5)); no private right of action
items.effective_or_amended: Effective January 1, 2026 (Created 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 72)

items.title: Prohibited uses of personally identifiable student information by cloud computing service provider
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds a "cloud computing service provider" -- any person other than an educational institution that operates a cloud computing service marketed/designed to provide a K-12 educational institution with account-based access to online computing resources.
key_obligations: A cloud computing service provider shall not process student data for any purpose other than providing, improving, developing, or maintaining the integrity of its cloud computing services, unless the parent expressly permits otherwise (KRS 365.734(2))
A provider may assist an educational institution with FERPA-permitted educational research (KRS 365.734(2))

A provider shall not in any case process student data to advertise, facilitate advertising, or create/correct an individual or household profile for advertising purposes, and shall not sell, disclose, or otherwise process student data for any commercial purpose (KRS 365.734(2))
A provider that contracts to provide cloud computing services to an educational institution must certify in writing that it will comply with subsection (2) (KRS 365.734(3))
The Kentucky Board of Education may promulgate administrative regulations to carry out the section (KRS 365.734(4))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Student data" includes the student's name, email address/messages, postal address, phone number, documents, photos, and unique identifiers relating to the student, created or provided in the course of using the cloud computing service (KRS 365.734(1)(f)).
items.effective_or_amended: Effective July 15, 2014 (Created 2014 Ky. Acts ch. 84, sec. 2)

items.title: Database Security Breach Notification Law
items.citation: La. R.S. 51:3071 et seq. (notification requirements at R.S. 51:3074)
items.applies_to_vendor: Any agency or person that maintains computerized data that includes personal information the agency/person does not own shall notify the owner or licensee of the information if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person through a breach, following discovery (R.S. 51:3074(D)).
key_obligations: A person/agency that owns or licenses computerized personal information must implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the information (R.S. 51:3074(A))
The owner/licensee must notify affected Louisiana residents following discovery of a breach (R.S. 51:3074(C))
A vendor/agency maintaining data it does not own must notify the owner or licensee of any breach following its own discovery (R.S. 51:3074(D))
Notification under Subsections C and D must be made in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but not later than 60 days from discovery of the breach (R.S. 51:3074(E))

If notice is delayed under the law-enforcement exception or to determine breach scope, the person/agency must give the Attorney General the reasons for delay in writing within the 60-day notification period; the AG may then allow a reasonable extension (R.S. 51:3074(E))

Notification is not required if, after a reasonable investigation, the person/business determines no reasonable likelihood of harm to residents exists; the written determination and supporting documentation must be retained for 5 years and sent to the AG within 30 days of a written request (R.S. 51:3074(I))
A violation of the Chapter is an unfair act or practice under R.S. 51:1405(A) (R.S. 51:3074(J))
items.notice_deadline: "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay but not later than sixty days from the discovery of the breach" (R.S. 51:3074(E))
items.regulator_notice: Where notice is delayed, the person/agency must give the Attorney General written reasons for the delay within the 60-day notification period (R.S. 51:3074(E)); the official statute text fetched this session does not contain a separate standalone "notify the AG within 10 days / $5,000 fine" provision, though that specific requirement is widely cited in secondary sources -- see uncertainty.
items.penalties: A violation constitutes an unfair act or practice under the Louisiana Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law, R.S. 51:1405(A) (R.S. 51:3074(J)); a civil action for actual damages from untimely notice is separately available under R.S. 51:3075
items.effective_or_amended: Acts 2005, No. 499, §1, eff. Jan. 1, 2006; last amended Acts 2018, No. 382, §1

items.citation: La. R.S. 51:1780.1 through 1780.5 (Chapter 20-B of Title 51), enacted by 2026 Act No. 502 (SB 386)
items.applies_to_vendor: Defines and regulates "processors" (persons that process personal data on behalf of a controller); processors must adhere to controller instructions, and a written contract between controller and processor governs the processor's data processing (per the enrolled bill's controller/processor duties provisions).
key_obligations: Applies only to a person/entity doing business in Louisiana that: has annual gross revenues over $25 million; OR annually buys, receives, sells, or shares personal information of 75,000+ consumers/households/devices; OR derives 50%+ of annual revenue from selling consumers' personal information (§1780.2(A))

items.title: Student information; privacy; legislative intent; definitions; prohibitions; parental access; penalties
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to "contractors" that a city, parish, or other local public school board contracts with for student and other education services, to whom student information (including personally identifiable information and cumulative records) may be transferred.
key_obligations: No contractor shall use student information to conduct predictive modeling for the purpose of limiting the educational opportunities of students
No contractor shall sell, transfer, share, or process any student data for use in commercial advertising or marketing, or any other commercial purpose, outside the scope of the service contract
No contractor shall allow access to, release, or allow the release of student information to any person or entity except as specified in the contract

Contracts with student-data contractors must include access guidelines, privacy compliance standards, security audit provisions, breach procedures, data retention policies, and a requirement to dispose of all information from the contractor's servers upon contract termination

Schools are prohibited from requiring collection of certain sensitive categories from students (political affiliations, psychological problems, sexual behavior/attitudes, illegal behavior, religious practices, family income, biometric information, gun ownership, home IP addresses)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Distinguishes "personally identifiable information" (data that can identify, contact, or locate a single individual -- names, SSNs, biometric records, medical/educational/financial data) from "aggregate data" (statistical information about groups from which individual identities cannot be distinguished).
items.penalties: Standard violations: up to 6 months imprisonment or a $10,000 fine; contractor violations: up to 3 years imprisonment or a $10,000 fine
items.effective_or_amended: Enacted 2014 (HB 1076)

items.title: Duty to report known security breach or unauthorized use of personal information
items.applies_to_vendor: A person or agency that maintains or stores, but does not own or license, data that includes personal information about a Massachusetts resident (a data processor/vendor) must provide notice when it knows or has reason to know of a breach of security or unauthorized use of personal information, notifying the owner or licensor of the information.
key_obligations: A person/agency must provide notice of a breach or unauthorized use of personal information as soon as practicable and without unreasonable delay, upon discovering it or being notified of it

A data processor/vendor that maintains but does not own the data must notify the data owner or licensor of the breach, including the breach details, approximate date, nature of the incident, and steps taken or planned (it need not disclose confidential business information or trade secrets)
The data owner/licensor must notify both the Attorney General and the Director of the Office of Consumer Affairs and Business Regulation (OCABR), as well as affected residents, for every breach

The regulator notice must include the nature of the breach, number of Massachusetts residents affected, types of compromised data (e.g., SSN, driver's license, financial account numbers), whether a written information security program exists, and remedial steps taken or planned
Consumer notice, unlike the regulator notice, must NOT include the nature of the breach or the number of residents affected
A breach involving Social Security numbers triggers mandatory free credit monitoring for at least 18 months under §3A
items.notice_deadline: "as soon as practicable and without unreasonable delay" -- no fixed day count in the statute
items.regulator_notice: Notice to both the Massachusetts Attorney General and the Director of the Office of Consumer Affairs and Business Regulation is required for every breach, regardless of the number of residents affected
items.personal_info_definition_notes: Massachusetts recognizes an encryption safe harbor: data encrypted with 128-bit or higher algorithms, where the encryption key was not also compromised, falls outside the breach definition.

items.title: Standards for the Protection of Personal Information of Residents of the Commonwealth (Written Information Security Program)
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to "all persons that own or license personal information about a resident of the Commonwealth," which by definition includes any vendor/processor (a "person" under 201 CMR 17.02 is any entity other than a Commonwealth government agency) that receives, stores, maintains, or processes such data in connection with providing goods or services -- and separately, §17.03(2)(f) requires such persons to flow the same security obligations down to their own third-party "service providers" by contract.
key_obligations: Every person that owns or licenses personal information about a Massachusetts resident must develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program (WISP) with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards appropriate to the size/scope/type of the business, its resources, the amount of stored data, and the need for security and confidentiality (§17.03(1))

The WISP must designate an employee to maintain it, identify and assess internal/external risks, set employee policies for records storage/access/transport, impose disciplinary measures, and prevent terminated employees from accessing personal information (§17.03(2)(a)-(e))

The person must take reasonable steps to select and retain third-party service providers capable of maintaining appropriate security measures consistent with 201 CMR 17.00, and must require such service providers by contract to implement and maintain those safeguards (§17.03(2)(f))
The WISP must impose reasonable physical-access restrictions and locked storage, regular monitoring, at-least-annual review, and documented post-incident review after any breach (§17.03(2)(g)-(j))

Where personal information is stored or transmitted electronically, the program must include secure user authentication, secure access controls, encryption of records transmitted across public networks or wirelessly, encryption of personal information on laptops/portable devices, up-to-date firewalls and OS patches, up-to-date malware protection, and employee training (§17.04)
Full compliance was required on or before March 1, 2010 (§17.05)
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Personal information" mirrors the c.93H definition: a MA resident's first name/initial and last name combined with SSN, driver's license/state ID number, or financial account/credit/debit card number (with or without a required access code) -- excluding lawfully public information.
items.effective_or_amended: Promulgated under M.G.L. c. 93H; compliance deadline March 1, 2010 (§17.05); the pre-March-2010 contract grandfathering language in §17.03(2)(f)2 shows the regulation's last substantive text change predates 2012

Checked for a Massachusetts SOPIPA-style student-data-privacy statute binding ed-tech operators/vendors, comparable to what Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, and Maryland have. None was found. Massachusetts instead relies on M.G.L. c. 71, §§34D-34H (which direct the Board of Elementary and Secondary Education to adopt regulations on maintenance, retention, duplication, storage, and destruction of student records -- a records-management mandate on schools, not an operator/vendor data-use statute) and the implementing regulation 603 CMR 23.00 (Student Records), neither of which directly restricts a third-party ed-tech vendor's use, sale, or targeted-advertising practices the way a SOPIPA-style law does. items.title: Maryland Personal Information Protection Act -- Security breach
items.applies_to_vendor: A business that maintains computerized personal information of a Maryland resident that it does not own or license must notify the owner or licensee of the information of a breach of security as soon as practicable, but not later than 10 days after the business discovers or is notified of the breach (§14-3504(b)).
key_obligations: A business that owns, licenses, or maintains computerized personal information of a Maryland resident must conduct a good-faith, reasonable and prompt investigation upon discovering or being notified of a breach, to determine the likelihood personal information has been or will be misused

If misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, the business must notify affected individuals as soon as reasonably practicable, but not later than 45 days after discovering or being notified of the breach
A business maintaining personal information it does not own must notify the owner or licensee within 10 days after discovering or being notified of the breach (§14-3504(b))

The business must notify the Maryland Attorney General before notifying affected individuals, including the number of affected residents, a description of the breach and timeline, remedial steps, and sample notification language
If a business determines after investigation that notification is not required, it must retain records of that determination for 3 years
items.notice_deadline: "as soon as reasonably practicable, but not later than 45 days after the business discovers or is notified of the breach" for consumer notice; "not later than 10 days" for the vendor-to-owner notice duty
items.regulator_notice: The business must notify the Maryland Attorney General before notifying affected individuals; the statute text retrieved this session does not state a numeric threshold below which AG notice is excused
items.personal_info_definition_notes: The statute cross-references the definition in §14-3501(e)(1) rather than defining "personal information" within §14-3504 itself.
items.penalties: A violation of the subtitle is an unfair or deceptive trade practice under Title 13 of the Commercial Law Article, and is subject to the enforcement and penalty provisions of Title 13 (§14-3508)

items.title: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act (MODPA)
items.citation: Md. Code Ann., Com. Law §§ 14-4701 through 14-4714 (Subtitle 47, recodified from Subtitle 46 §§14-4601-14-4614)
items.applies_to_vendor: Requires that if a controller uses a processor to process personal data of consumers, the controller and processor must enter into a binding contract governing the processor's data processing procedures on the controller's behalf (§14-4708).
key_obligations: Applies to a person that conducts business in Maryland or provides products/services targeted to Maryland residents, and during the preceding calendar year controlled/processed personal data of at least 35,000 consumers (excluding data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or controlled/processed personal data of at least 10,000 consumers while deriving more than 20% of gross revenue from selling personal data (§14-4702)
Controller and processor must enter into a binding contract clearly setting out processing procedures for data processed on the controller's behalf (§14-4708(a))

If a third party uses or shares a consumer's information inconsistent with promises made at collection, it must notify the affected consumer of the new/changed practice before implementing it (§14-4709)
Controllers must conduct data protection assessments for processing activities that present a heightened risk of harm, including targeted advertising (§14-4710)

A violation of the subtitle is an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under Title 13 of the Commercial Law Article and subject to Title 13's enforcement/penalty provisions, except §13-408 (§14-4713)
The Division may issue a notice of violation and offer a cure opportunity for enforcement actions concerning alleged violations occurring on or before April 1, 2027 (§14-4714)
items.regulator_notice: Before initiating an enforcement action for a violation occurring on or before April 1, 2027, the Division may issue a notice of violation to the controller/processor if it determines a cure is possible (§14-4714(b))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Sensitive data" and "biometric data" definitions are set out at §14-4701; biometric data expressly excludes ordinary photographs and audio/video recordings unless generated to identify a specific consumer.
items.penalties: Enforced as an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under Title 13 of the Commercial Law Article (the Maryland Consumer Protection Act), except the private-right-of-action provision at §13-408 (§14-4713)
items.effective_or_amended: Enacted 2024 (Chapters 454 and 455); effective October 1, 2025

items.title: Student Data Privacy Act
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds an "operator": an individual or entity operating under the school-official exception of FERPA, per a contract or agreement with a Maryland public school or local school system, that provides an internet website/online service/online application/mobile application processing covered information for a PreK-12 school purpose.
key_obligations: An operator shall protect covered information from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure, and implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices (§4-131(c))
An operator shall delete covered information within a reasonable time if a public school or local school system under whose authority the data sits requests deletion (§4-131(c)(3))
An operator may not knowingly engage in targeted advertising based on covered information or persistent unique identifiers acquired through its site/service/application (§4-131(d)(1)(i))
An operator may not use covered information to make a profile about a student, except in furtherance of a PreK-12 school purpose (§4-131(d)(1)(ii))
An operator may not sell a student's information, subject to a business-transfer exception (§4-131(d)(1)(iii))

An operator may not disclose covered information except for enumerated purposes: PreK-12 school purpose with restricted recipient use, legal/regulatory compliance, liability precautions, judicial process, safety/security, contractually-bound service providers, legal compliance, legitimate research, or to a state/local education agency (§4-131(d)(1)(iv), (e))
If an operator is merged with or acquired by another entity, the successor entity remains subject to the section for previously collected covered information (§4-131(f))
items.personal_info_definition_notes: "Covered information" is broadly defined to include educational records, contact info, geolocation, test results/grades, special education and criminal records, medical/health records, SSN, biometric information, socioeconomic data, food purchases, political/religious affiliations, text messages, search activity, photos, voice recordings, disciplinary information, online behavior, and persistent unique identifiers linked to a student (§4-131(a)(2)).
items.effective_or_amended: Student Data Privacy Act of 2015; substantially amended 2022 (Chapter 164, HB 769)

items.title: Notice of Risk to Personal Data Act
items.applies_to_vendor: A third-party entity holding data on behalf of another "information broker" or person must notify the person maintaining the personal information of a breach immediately following discovery, if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person.

A third-party entity that holds data on behalf of another must notify the person maintaining the personal information of a breach immediately following discovery
The entity must notify either the appropriate state regulator within the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation, or -- if unregulated by that department -- the Attorney General

Entities discovering breaches affecting more than 1,000 persons must also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies without unreasonable delay, including the breach date and estimated number affected

items.regulator_notice: Notify either the applicable regulator within the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation, or the Attorney General if the entity is not regulated by that department

items.title: Student Information Privacy Act -- Restrictions on operator's use of student data
items.applies_to_vendor: Binds an "operator": any entity (other than the Department, a school administrative unit, or a school) that operates an internet website, online service, or application designed and marketed for K-12 school purposes.
key_obligations: An operator may not knowingly sell student data without explicit written or electronic parental/eligible-student consent (§953(1))

items.title: Identity Theft Protection Act — notice of security breach

key_obligations: A person/agency that owns or licenses data must notify each affected MI resident whose unencrypted personal information was accessed and acquired, unless the breach is determined not likely to cause substantial loss/injury or identity theft (MCL 445.72(1), (3)).
A person/agency that maintains data it does not own must notify the owner/licensor of the breach (MCL 445.72(2)) — this is the vendor duty.
Notice must be given without unreasonable delay, subject to a law-enforcement or scope-investigation delay exception (MCL 445.72(4)).
If notifying more than 1,000 MI residents, must also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies without unreasonable delay (MCL 445.72(8)).
Entities already compliant with GLBA or HIPAA breach-notice rules are deemed compliant (MCL 445.72(9), (10)).

items.personal_info_definition_notes: Defined elsewhere in the Act (MCL 445.63); 445.72 covers unencrypted/unredacted personal information, or encrypted information accessed together with the encryption key.
items.penalties: Fraudulent false notice: misdemeanor, up to 93 days imprisonment and $250/$500/$750 fines for 1st/2nd/3rd+ violations (MCL 445.72(12)). Knowing failure to provide required notice: civil fine up to $250 per failure, aggregate capped at $750,000 per breach event, recoverable by the AG or a prosecuting attorney (MCL 445.72(13)-(14)). Separately, MCL 445.72a (data destruction on removal from database) carries a misdemeanor fine up to $250 per violation.

items.title: SHIELD Act — reasonable data security safeguards requirement
items.applies_to_vendor: Applies to "any person or business that owns or licenses computerized data which includes private information of a resident of New York" — a broad standard that reaches a vendor like LOVELEEDAY whenever it holds NY-resident private information for its own operational purposes (e.g., as a controller of its own client/vendor records), and which independently requires any covered business to oversee its own service providers' safeguards by contract.
key_obligations: Must develop, implement, and maintain a data security program with reasonable administrative safeguards: designate employee(s) to coordinate the program, identify reasonably foreseeable internal/external risks, train employees, require safeguards from service providers by contract, and adjust the program as the business changes

Must implement reasonable technical safeguards: assess risk in network/software design and in information processing, transmission, and storage; detect, prevent, and respond to attacks; regularly test and monitor controls

Must implement reasonable physical safeguards: assess risk of information storage/disposal, detect/prevent/respond to intrusions, protect against unauthorized access, and dispose of data so it cannot be read or reconstructed
Small businesses (fewer than 50 employees, under $3M annual revenue, or under $5M in assets) must implement safeguards "appropriate for the size and complexity" of their own operations
Violations are treated as a GBL § 349 violation, enforceable by the Attorney General for injunctive relief and civil penalties under § 350-d; the section creates no private right of action

items.title: Notice of breach of security of computerized personal information
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §46A-2A-102(c), an individual or entity that maintains computerized data including personal information that it does not own or license shall give notice to the owner or licensee of the information of any breach as soon as practicable following discovery, if the personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, accessed and acquired by an unauthorized person.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify data owner: 'as soon as practicable following discovery' (§46A-2A-102(c))
Owner/licensee must notify affected residents 'without unreasonable delay' following discovery/notification of the breach (§46A-2A-102(a))
If more than 1,000 persons must be notified, also notify nationwide consumer reporting agencies without unreasonable delay (§46A-2A-102(f))
No statutory Attorney General pre-notice/threshold requirement found in this article
Failure to comply is an unfair or deceptive act under W. Va. Code § 46A-6-104, enforceable exclusively by the Attorney General absent willful repeated violations (§46A-2A-104)
items.notice_deadline: 'without unreasonable delay' for individual notice; 'as soon as practicable' for vendor-to-owner notice; no fixed day count in the statute
items.personal_info_definition_notes: First name/initial + last name linked to unencrypted, unredacted SSN, driver's license/state ID number, or financial account/card number with security code (§46A-2A-101).
items.penalties: AG has exclusive enforcement authority; civil penalty only on a court finding of repeated and willful violations, not to exceed $150,000 per breach or series of similar breaches discovered in a single investigation (§46A-2A-104(b))

HB 5123 (a 2026 reintroduction) also failed to advance before the legislature adjourned sine die March 14, 2026. West Virginia residents rely on the state breach law (W. Va. Code § 46A-2A) plus federal frameworks (HIPAA, GLBA, COPPA, FERPA). items.title: Student Data Accessibility, Transparency and Accountability Act
items.applies_to_vendor: This statute is primarily directed at the West Virginia Department of Education/school districts rather than establishing direct operator prohibitions (unlike SOPIPA-style laws in TX/UT/VT/VA/WA). It binds vendors indirectly: the Department must ensure any contract with a private vendor governing databases, assessments, or instructional supports that include student or redacted data 'include[s] express provisions that safeguard privacy and security and include[s] penalties for noncompliance' (§18-2-5h(c)(6)), and must ensure vendor compliance with a data security plan (encryption, breach planning/notification, retention/disposition policies) (§18-2-5h(c)(4)).
key_obligations: Confidential student information (SSN, religious affiliation, firearm ownership, medical/psychological/behavioral diagnoses, criminal history, biometric data, genetic information, etc., defined at §18-2-5h(b)(11)) may not be transferred to any outside entity except under listed exceptions
Department contracts with vendors for databases/assessments/instructional supports must include express privacy/security safeguards and noncompliance penalties (§18-2-5h(c)(6))

Department must maintain a data security plan covering access authentication, privacy compliance/audits, breach planning and notification, data retention/disposition, and encryption/employee-training safeguards (§18-2-5h(c)(4))
Parents must be notified 'as soon as possible' after a suspected or confirmed data security breach (§18-2-5h(c)(8))
Collection of confidential student information is prohibited outright (§18-2-5h(c)(9))
items.notice_deadline: Parents notified 'as soon as possible' after a suspected or confirmed breach
items.regulator_notice: Governor must be notified upon suspicion or confirmation of a breach, and at regular intervals while it is managed
items.personal_info_definition_notes: 'Confidential student information' is broadly defined (§18-2-5h(b)(11)) and separately restricted from district-level reporting to the state (§18-2-5h(d)): juvenile delinquency records, criminal records, medical/health records, student biometric information.
items.penalties: Statute requires vendor contracts to include penalties for noncompliance, but does not itself set a statutory penalty amount for vendor violations
items.effective_or_amended: Amended 2017 (SB 656); originally 2014 (HB 4316), amended 2016 (HB 4261)
items.uncertainty: This is a DOE/school-district-facing statute with a contractual flow-down to vendors, not a direct SOPIPA-style operator-prohibition statute (contrast TX/UT/VT/VA/WA items) — noted so it is not mistaken for the same obligation shape.

items.title: Computer security breach; notice to affected persons
items.applies_to_vendor: Under §40-12-502(g), any person who maintains computerized data that includes personal identifying information on behalf of another business entity shall disclose to that business entity any breach of the security of the system as soon as practicable following the determination that the information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person. The maintaining person and the business entity may agree who provides the single required notice; absent agreement, the party with the direct resident relationship must notify.
key_obligations: Vendor/maintainer duty to notify the business entity: 'as soon as practicable following the determination' that data was or is believed acquired (§40-12-502(g))

On becoming aware of a breach, conduct a good-faith, reasonable, prompt investigation into likely misuse; if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, give notice 'as soon as possible' to affected Wyoming residents, in the 'most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay' (§40-12-502(a))

No statutory Wyoming Attorney General pre-notice/threshold requirement — the AG's role under §40-12-502(f) is enforcement authority (civil action for violations), not a recipient of a mandatory breach notice
Financial institutions and HIPAA-covered entities/business associates that comply with their federal breach regimes are deemed compliant (§40-12-502(c), (h))
items.notice_deadline: 'as soon as possible' / 'most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement' — no fixed day count in the statute
items.personal_info_definition_notes: First name/initial + last name combined with one or more data elements specified in Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-901(b)(iii)–(xiv), when not redacted (§40-12-501(a)(vii)); excludes information lawfully available from government records or widely distributed media (§40-12-501(b)).
items.penalties: §40-12-502(f): the Attorney General may bring an action in law or equity to address a violation and recover damages or other appropriate relief; no fixed statutory civil-penalty dollar amount is set for breach-notice violations (the $1,000/violation penalty at §40-12-508 applies only to security-freeze violations, a different part of the same chapter)

Wyoming relies on its Consumer Protection Act, the breach-notification statute (Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-501 et seq.), and federal law.
